data.title: Q3 2026 U.S. Retail Scorecard - Update
data.description:
To date, 149 of the 183 companies in our LSEG Retail/Restaurant Index have reported their EPS results for Q3 2026, representing 81% of the index. Of those companies that have reported their quarterly results, 69% announced profits that beat analysts’ expectations, while 3% delivered on-target results and 28% reported earnings that fell below estimates. The Q3 2026 blended earnings growth estimate now stands at 8.7%.

The blended revenue growth estimate for the 146 companies in this index is 6.4% for Q3 2026. Of those companies that have reported their quarterly results so far, 59% announced revenue that exceeded analysts’ expectations and the remaining 41% reported that their revenue fell below analysts’ forecasts.

Exhibit 1: LSEG Earnings Dashboard

This week in retail

Walmart (WMT) delivered another robust quarter, exceeding earnings, revenue, and same store sales (SSS) expectations. Earnings increased 4.8% from a year ago, while revenue rose 5.2%. U.S. comparable sales increased 2.9%, although the result was affected by federal Medicare drug-pricing rules. Excluding that impact, comparable sales would have risen approximately 3.6%, suggesting underlying consumer demand was stronger than the headline figure indicates.

Sales growth was broad-based across categories, supported by continued market-share gains and a 23% surge in U.S. e-commerce, driven by strong pickup and delivery demand. Meanwhile, Walmart Connect — its U.S. advertising business — grew 37%, while global membership fee revenue increased 17%. Together, these higher-margin businesses provide Walmart with additional financial flexibility to invest in lower prices, strengthen customer loyalty and expand its competitive advantage.

The results reinforce a key theme this earnings season: consumers are still spending, but they are shopping more strategically. Both customer traffic and average ticket increased, while Walmart continued to gain market share across income groups, including households earning more than $100,000 annually. This suggests that value-seeking behavior is extending beyond lower-income shoppers, as even higher-income consumers become increasingly selective about where they spend.

E-commerce remains a particularly powerful growth engine. Walmart’s 23% digital growth reinforces a broader trend across retail, with Target (TGT), Home Depot (HD), and Lowe’s (LOW) also reporting strong online sales. The results suggest that convenience, faster fulfillment, and competitive pricing are increasingly influencing consumer purchasing decisions, making digital capabilities a critical differentiator in today’s retail environment.

Meanwhile, Williams-Sonoma (WSM) matched Q3 earnings expectations, with earnings increasing 11.6% from a year ago and revenue rising 5.8%. Comparable sales grew a healthy 5.1%, supported by positive performance across its brands and channels. The results highlight continued resilience among some higher-income consumers who remain willing to spend on premium home furnishings despite broader economic uncertainty.

Management emphasized the strength of its differentiated merchandise and operating model, noting that its design capabilities and direct sourcing strategy have supported increased full-price selling while maintaining a compelling value proposition. This combination of product differentiation, pricing discipline and operational efficiency helped support profitability during the quarter.

Williams-Sonoma also benefited from tariff-related income, which helped offset higher costs of goods sold, as well as increased interest income. Encouraged by its performance, the home furnishings retailer reiterated its fiscal 2026 outlook, signaling confidence in its ability to sustain momentum through the holiday season.

StarMine Signals Potential Earnings Surprises at Five Below (FIVE) and Ross Stores (ROST)

Looking ahead, value remains a dominant theme this earnings season, with consumers increasingly prioritizing affordability, compelling merchandise, and a differentiated shopping experience. Against this backdrop, LSEG StarMine models identify Five Below and Ross Stores as potential earnings outperformers heading into their upcoming Q3 announcements.

Sentiment is particularly favorable for Five Below, with consensus estimates calling for Q3 2026 EPS of $1.17 and SSS growth of 10.8%. More importantly, the StarMine Predicted Surprise exceeds 2%, signaling an elevated likelihood that the value retailer could outperform consensus earnings expectations and deliver a positive surprise (Exhibit 2).

Similarly, StarMine signals suggest that Ross Stores is well positioned to exceed earnings expectations, supported by continued demand for discounted branded merchandise. With consumers increasingly focused on stretching their purchasing power, the upcoming results from both retailers will provide further insight into the strength of discretionary spending and the competitive positioning of value-oriented retailers.

data.title: Indian Rupee Hits Fresh Seven-Month Low On Strong FIIs Buying Momentum
data.description:
• The Indian Rupee posts a fresh seven-month high against the US Dollar, with the USD/INR pair sliding to near 92.70.

  • Indian stock market continues to attract foreign money on the back of lower oil prices and global AI unwinding.

  • The US Dollar Index extends its rally amid a hawkish Fed narrative.

The Indian Rupee (INR) extends its upside run against the US Dollar (USD) on Friday, strengthened by the continuous inflow of foreign funds amid global Artificial Intelligence (AI) unwinding and lower oil prices.

During the day, the USD/INR pair posts a fresh seven-month low near 92.70.

On Thursday, Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) remain net buyers in the Indian stock market again and raised their stake in equities worth Rs. 7,411.41 crore. So far in November, FIIs has made investments worth Rs. 1,01,640.97 crore.

What has improved India’s appeal in recent weeks?

According to The Economic Times (ET), India has been described as an “anti-AI” trade because it was left out of much of the global AI rally and has limited direct exposure to the AI supply chain. Any unwinding of crowded AI-linked positions could therefore encourage investors to rotate into other emerging markets, including India and Brazil.

Analysts at DBS said in a note that “regional equity plays that have been relatively less exposed to the AI-play this year appear to be benefiting in the initial phase of re-allocation”.

Meanwhile, lower oil prices due to rising supply of energy products from the Middle East have also increased the appeal of India.

In the opening trade, the MCX Crude Oil contract expiring on December 18 is close to its over 11-week low of Rs. 7,619 posted on Wednesday.

Strategists at Danske Bank highlight that the recent sell-off in crude has been substantial, with “oil prices… down around 20% this month,” as the market responds to “recovering supply from the Middle East” and growing “expectations that US President Donald Trump will avoid renewed full-scale hostilities with Iran.”

Investors shrug off rally in US Dollar

The continuous rally in the Indian Rupee against the US Dollar despite the US Dollar Index (DXY) hitting fresh highs every trading day in over a week reflects sheer strength in the Indian currency.

As of writing, the USD Index is marginally lower to near 103.78 from its fresh 19-month high of around 104.00 posted the previous day.

Analysts at MUFG/BTMU note that “almost all Fed officials have judged that additional rate hikes would likely be appropriate in the months ahead to bring inflation back to the 2% target.” They add that “markets continue to fully price in a 25bps hike in December, three 25bps hikes by June next year, leaving elevated US rates and a resilient Dollar.

Technical Analysis: USD/INR sees more downside towards 92.50

In the daily chart, USD/INR trades at 92.71, maintaining a bearish near-term tone as it holds beneath the nine-period exponential moving average (EMA) at 93.57. The pair continues to slide away from this dynamic resistance, while the Relative Strength Index (RSI) at 22.6 sits in oversold territory, hinting that downside momentum is stretched but not yet reversed.

On the topside, the 9-period EMA at 93.57 is the first resistance to clear for any recovery attempt, and a sustained move above this level would ease immediate bearish pressure. On the downside, the pair could extend its decline towards 92.20.

data.title: The AI Bubble Is Draining Market Liquidity, But Gold’s Fundamentals Remain Robust
data.description:
In my October 30 article, titled “The AI bubble is draining capital from other markets, including gold”, I explained how the artificial intelligence industry had become an enormous magnet for capital. Hundreds of billions of dollars were being mobilized to finance infrastructure whose future profitability remained largely unproven, while small-cap companies, industrial businesses and mining stocks were struggling to attract investors.

I focused on an especially dangerous mechanism: the market valuations of AI-related companies no longer simply reflected their growth prospects; they were gradually becoming an essential condition for financing that growth. The higher share prices climbed, the more capital these companies could raise to fund new data centers, thereby sustaining stock-market euphoria.

But this mechanism also works in reverse.

When valuations begin to fall, financing capacity deteriorates, lenders reassess the collateral available to them, and companies that depend most heavily on capital markets are forced to rethink their ambitions. This is precisely the risk we had identified.

The governance crisis currently engulfing Nvidia adds a new dimension to this vulnerability. Jensen Huang’s resignation, followed by statements hinting at a possible return, prompted an unusual show of activity in Silicon Valley. However, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent publicly argued in favor of appointing a successor from outside the company, amid questions about technological ties with China.

Beyond the circumstances of this departure, which still require clarification, the situation highlights just how strategically important Nvidia has become to the United States. Jensen Huang was not simply running a semiconductor manufacturer: he embodied an ecosystem in which suppliers, customers and investors have increasingly close financial ties.

The market correction now gives us a sense of the risks involved. Since its October 6 peak, Nvidia has lost around $2 trillion in market capitalization, with its valuation falling from approximately $5.8 trillion to $3.8 trillion.

Of course, this does not mean that $2 trillion in cash has actually left the markets. But this destruction of financial wealth can reduce the value of assets used as collateral, limit investors’ borrowing capacity and trigger forced selling across other asset classes.

This is how a stock-market correction concentrated in a handful of major technology companies can gradually turn into a broad-based contraction in liquidity.

The Fed cannot offset the destruction of financial wealth

Some investors are now counting on the Federal Reserve to stabilize the markets. Yet the amounts involved illustrate the limits of monetary intervention.

The Fed plans to reinvest around $14 billion in Treasury securities between November 16 and December 11, a negligible amount compared with the $2 trillion wiped off Nvidia’s market capitalization. These figures are not directly comparable, of course, since the Fed’s reinvestments are not intended to offset stock-market losses. However, they give an idea of the gap between the monetary operations currently planned and the scale of the ongoing repricing of financial assets.

More importantly, providing reserves to banks does not necessarily restore their appetite for risk. A bank may have ample liquidity and still refuse to finance a data-center operator whose collateral is losing value.

The problem is particularly concerning for neocloud providers, whose business models depend on continuously securing new financing. CoreWeave bonds are reportedly now yielding close to 15%, while certain Nebius convertible bonds are trading at around 70% of their face value.

With borrowing costs rising so sharply, profitability prospects could deteriorate quickly. The major hyperscalers still have balance sheets strong enough to absorb some of this pressure, but the most heavily indebted operators could find themselves in a much more difficult position.

Here we see the same mechanisms that emerged during the telecom bubble: a genuine technological revolution, but infrastructure financed on the basis of growth and profitability assumptions that the markets eventually begin to question.

The question is no longer simply how many GPUs Nvidia will be able to sell, but who will still be able to borrow the money to buy them, and at what cost.

Gold is correcting under liquidity pressure, but demand remains resilient

The recent correction in precious metals needs to be understood in this context.

In October, gold fell 6.8%, ending the month at around $3,875 an ounce, while silver lost 18.7% and the leading gold-mining stocks declined by nearly 12%.

At first glance, this may seem paradoxical. Concerns about financing the AI industry, deteriorating credit conditions and mounting sovereign-debt tensions should, in theory, make gold more attractive.

But when a stock-market correction triggers deleveraging, investors do not sell only the losing positions. They also dump their most liquid assets to rebuild cash reserves and meet margin calls.

Gold then becomes a source of liquidity to cover losses incurred elsewhere.

We saw this phenomenon in 2008 and again in March 2020. In both cases, gold initially corrected during the broad liquidation phase before regaining its role as a safe haven when central banks were forced to intervene.

But one feature sets the current correction apart: falling prices have not been accompanied by a collapse in investment demand.

At the end of October, gold-backed ETF holdings stood at around 100.97 million ounces, even surpassing their February levels. Silver-backed ETFs also recorded an increase in their physical holdings, adding nearly 4.9 million ounces over the month.

In other words, prices fell sharply while the quantities of metal held by these investment vehicles remained resilient.

This divergence suggests that the correction has been driven more by position adjustments in derivatives markets, systematic strategies and short-term liquidity needs than by a broad withdrawal of long-term investors.

Quantitative funds and trend-following strategies, in particular, reduced their exposure to gold as certain technical thresholds were breached. According to some estimates, these market participants’ short positions were already approaching their usual limits by mid-October.

This development matters. Once excessive speculative positioning has been largely unwound, the market may become more sensitive to an improvement in financial conditions, although this does not necessarily mean that a bottom has already been reached.

China is absorbing some of the selling from Western markets

Another revealing factor is the behavior of Chinese buyers.

While Western investors were reducing their exposure to gold, premiums in Shanghai remained high, pointing to physical demand capable of absorbing some of the metal being sold internationally.

The divergence between the two markets has become striking. Over a rolling ten-week period, the correlation between an indicator combining Western gold positioning and Shanghai premiums is said to have fallen to around −0.97.

This figure does not mean that China mechanically absorbs every ounce sold in the West. Nevertheless, it shows that the two indicators have recently moved in almost opposite directions: while Western financial investors were reducing their positions, premiums in the Chinese market pointed to sustained physical demand.

This distinction between the financial market and the physical market is becoming essential.

On Western markets, prices are heavily influenced in the short term by futures contracts, options, quantitative strategies and portfolio arbitrage. In China, physical demand is driven more by concerns relating to wealth preservation, monetary considerations and savings diversification.

The persistent weakness of China’s property market, difficulties in domestic credit markets and uncertainty surrounding economic growth are prompting some savers to seek assets whose value does not depend directly on the solvency of a financial intermediary.

Gold also benefits from central banks’ desire to diversify their reserves in an increasingly fragmented geopolitical environment.

We are therefore seeing a revealing trend: Western investors might sell gold to obtain dollars, but other market participants buy gold precisely to reduce their dependence on those same dollars.

This divergence could become one of the market’s main sources of support once liquidation pressures begin to ease.

Sovereign debt is gradually reinforcing gold’s monetary role

The recent correction should not obscure the broader transformation in the macroeconomic environment.

In October, gold faced a particularly unfavorable combination of factors: rising US real interest rates, a stronger dollar, energy-related inflationary pressures and a tightening of global financial conditions.

The US 10-year real yield briefly approached 3%, while the nominal yield exceeded 5.3%. In such an environment, the higher opportunity cost of holding an asset that generates no income makes gold less attractive to some investors.

But this rise in interest rates also reveals a much deeper vulnerability.

Developed countries must finance substantial structural deficits even as the cost of their debt rises. France is a particularly worrying example: its 10-year sovereign yield exceeded 5%, while the yield spread over German bonds reached around 174 basis points at the end of October.

The problem extends well beyond France. The United States, the United Kingdom and Japan are facing, to varying degrees, higher financing needs and increased sensitivity of their public finances to interest rates.

For investors, this raises a fundamental question: can sovereign bonds continue to serve simultaneously as reserve assets, financial collateral and protection against crises?

When the sustainability of public debt itself becomes a source of concern, physical gold once again demonstrates the full relevance of one of its fundamental characteristics: it is not the liability of any government and does not depend on any issuer’s ability to repay its debt.

Silver and mining stocks: an even sharper correction

Silver suffered a much steeper correction than gold in October, falling by nearly 19%. This underperformance can be explained by a combination of contracting liquidity, the metal’s inherently higher volatility and its sensitivity to the outlook for industrial activity.

As a result, the gold-to-silver ratio has risen to around 79, well above its long-term historical average, generally estimated at 60:

This level is not in itself a buy signal, but it highlights the extent of silver’s relative underperformance.

The situation is all the more interesting because silver-backed ETF holdings increased during the correction. From their July lows, these investment vehicles are said to have accumulated nearly 19.5 million additional ounces by the end of October.

Some investors appear to be taking advantage of lower prices to increase their exposure to the metal, while derivatives markets continue to exert downward pressure on prices.

Mining stocks, for their part, remain particularly vulnerable during episodes of deleveraging. They combine exposure to metal prices with sensitivity to equity markets and, in the case of small-cap companies, often limited liquidity.

But this correction is also widening valuation gaps between companies with tangible assets, identified reserves and sometimes substantial cash flows, and technology companies whose valuations are still largely based on expectations of future revenue.

This divergence is likely to persist as long as investors continue to reduce their overall exposure to risk.

Nevertheless, it could pave the way for a much more favorable phase of capital reallocation toward real assets once financing pressures begin to ease.

The immediate risk for gold remains another wave of forced liquidations. But its main source of support over the medium term could lie precisely in the financial consequences of the AI bubble bursting.

The real question, then, is not simply how far technology stocks may fall, but when the contraction in liquidity will stop weighing on the gold price and begin to strengthen its role as a benchmark monetary asset.

data.title: Nasdaq 100 Tests Major Long-Term Support
data.description:
The Nasdaq 100 (QQQ) is sitting right on a major long-term support level. Holding the $636 to $637 area is crucial for any chance at a short-term bounce. And even if a bounce does come, there’s plenty of resistance stacked up above. The strongest of it is the short-term trend-line off the all-time highs.

How far has the Nasdaq 100 fallen?

QQQ topped out near $763 in early October. It’s now trading around $636, which puts it down roughly 17% from the highs. The Nasdaq 100 officially entered correction territory at the start of the month, and the selling hasn’t let up. Thursday’s 2% drop marked the sixth straight losing day for the S&P 500, and chip stocks fell around the world again overnight.

What stands out most to me is how the market handled Nvidia’s earnings. Nvidia more than doubled its revenue from a year ago and guided higher, and the stock still closed lower the next day. It isn’t uncommon for stocks to do that, but when a market sells off on great earnings, that tells you a lot about where sentiment is, especially when it entered earnings having already been hammered by investors and the stock market as a whole. And still, buyers aren’t in a hurry to step in yet.

Why is the $636 to $637 level so important for QQQ?

It’s the old ceiling. QQQ’s highs in November of last year and again in January both stalled right at this level, and the stock chopped around underneath it for months. It finally broke out in April and never looked back, until now.

That’s the classic setup where old resistance becomes new support, and this is the first time QQQ has come back to test it from above. It matters even more because QQQ already lost its rising trend-line off the April 2025 lows this week. If $636 to $637 gives way too, QQQ falls back inside that old trading range, and the bottom of that range is a long way down.

What resistance levels should you watch if QQQ bounces?

Even if this level holds, a bounce has a lot of work to do:

  1. The $655 to $661 area. This is where the broken trend-line from the April 2025 lows meets the late-July low. Both were support not long ago. Now they’re overhead.

  2. The 200-day moving average, around $683. QQQ sliced through it earlier this month.

  3. The short-term trend-line off the all-time highs. This is the one I’d watch most closely. QQQ has put in a series of lower highs since the October peak, and the line connecting them has capped every rally attempt so far. Until QQQ gets back above it, any bounce is just that, a bounce inside a downtrend.

How I’m trading QQQ here

If QQQ holds this level into the close, I’ll look for a bounce, but I’ll treat it as a trade, not a new uptrend. That means a tight stop just below support, and taking profits as it runs into the $655 to $661 area. I’m not expecting a V-shaped recovery while QQQ is still below that short-term trend-line.

If $636 to $637 breaks (which it is currently doing as of this writing), I stay defensive. There’s no reason to catch a falling knife, and cash is a position too.

It’s also monthly options expiration today, which can add some extra whipsaw, so I’ll wait for the close before reading too much into the intraday moves.

As I always say, Plan your trade, manage your risk, and the profits will take care of themselves.

data.title: Silver Price Forecast: Failed Recovery Leaves Market Vulnerable
data.description:
The silver market continues to see a lot of noisy trading, particularly to the downside, as there are major headwinds out there to keep the silver market down. The most obvious reason is real rates.

Silver

The silver market initially tried to rally during Thursday’s trading session but then gave back gains again as we tried to cross above the $45 level. The $48 level after that has a certain amount of resistance built into it as well, followed by the 50-day EMA. This is a market that really has no signs of strength, and there are various areas above that could cause massive issues.

Ultimately, this is a market that I think continues to see a lot of pressure, not only from possibly forced liquidations, but also because real rates in America continue to pay you quite well. If that is going to be the case, it is very likely that traders will be watching any rally as an opportunity to start shorting silver again.

The psychology of $50

The $50 level being broken through over the last couple of days is a big deal. That was a major ceiling for decades, which was just recently broken, and we are already below it again. I think silver has further to go to the downside. Clearly, there are no signs of real strength.

Longer term, I love silver. I think it will be a great investment. But right now, in this environment, until those real rates come down, it is going to be very difficult for silver to pick up strength. It is so sensitive to rates, even more so than gold. Of course, the strong U.S. dollar is doing it no favors as well, which is all intertwined. At this point, this is a market that remains fragile at best, horrible at worst.

data.title: Why Anthropic Could Get Ugly Next Week
data.description:
Anthropic (ANT) touched $83.47 this morning, and it bounced.

That’s no coincidence. Anthropic priced its IPO at $83 a share on Wednesday, and there’s a buyer sitting at that price whose whole job is to keep the stock from falling apart.

The Buyer With One Job

When a company goes public, one or more of the banks in the underwriting syndicate can act as what’s called a stabilization agent. If the shares start to sell off under the IPO price, the stabilization agent steps in and buys.

The rule is exact. It can’t buy a single share above $83. At $83 and below, it can nibble, and it can take on a lot of risk if this thing starts to come down.

And it’s not some guy behind a screen. It’s a computer system, an algorithm fighting the market at $83. If we hit 83 today, you’ll see it. The stock will come down, and they’ll punch it right back. Come down, punch it right back. I’ve traded around a stabilization algorithm before, about 25 years ago.

How Long Can They Hold The Line?

That depends on whether they have what’s called a green shoe. A green shoe lets the underwriters put more shares out to the market even weeks after the IPO if there’s demand. If they have one, the stabilization agent can stay in there for weeks or even months.

Monday Changes Everything

On Monday, options start trading on Anthropic, and a stabilization agent can’t do very much against an options market.

Right now, you can’t short the stock at home, because there’s no stock in the book to borrow. So traders who want to get short will buy puts, and buy puts, and buy puts. The market maker sells them those puts, then shorts the stock to reduce its own risk, because market makers are allowed to do that.

Once the options list, there’s no stability. This thing could drop to 50.

So set an alert on Anthropic at or below $83 today. If it gets there, watch the tape and see the algorithm punch it back. Then on Monday, watch what happens to that same level when the puts start trading.

data.description:
Open Text Corporation was founded in 1991 and is headquartered in Waterloo, Canada.

OTEX designs, develops, markets and sells enterprise information management software and solutions.

Three key data points gauge OTEX (or any dividend paying equity):

(1) Price 

(2) Dividends

(3) Returns

Those three keys also indicate if any company has made, is making, and will make money.

OTEX Price

Open Text’s single share price fell $10.18 (or 31.25%) in the past year, from $32.57 to $22.39 per Thursday’s opening market report.

Twelve analysts cover the stock. The median of their one year target price estimates pinned the price at $28.14 or $5.75 higher.

However, OTEX’s twenty year price progression from $4.60 in November 2006 to $22.39 at mid November 2026 showed an average annual gain of $0.885. 

I’ll use the average of analyst and twenty year historic annual estimates (or $3.32) to calculate returns after I discuss OTEX dividends.

OTEX Dividends

Open Text has paid quarterly dividends increasing annually since June, 2013.

The most recent Q dividend of $0.28 per share will pay out   December 18, to shareholders of record December 4th.  The resulting forward looking annual dividend of $1.12 yields 4.88% (per Thursday’s opening market report.)  

OTEX Returns

To get there, our $3.32  per share estimated potential annual price gain was added to the $1.12 presumed forward looking annual dividend to make that $4.41 gross gain.

By the way, one dividend dogcatcher guideline is to only buy initial shares of a dividend stock that pay an annual dividend (from $1000 invested) that is more than the cost of one share.

OTEX’s projected annual dividend from $1K invested is $48.80 and that annual dividend proves to be over 2.17 times  more than its Wednesday $22.39 single-share opening price. 

The exact track of Open Text Corporation’s future share price and dividend will entirely be determined by market action and company finances.

data.title: Pound Under Pressure As GBP/USD Tests Yearly Lows
data.description:
GBP/USD fell to 1.3085 on Friday, remaining at its lowest level in almost a year. The main pressure on the pound comes from sharply rising expectations of further Fed tightening, which is supporting the US dollar.

Minutes from the October Fed meeting showed that the Fed is increasingly concerned about persistent inflation and acknowledges the need for additional rate hikes. Policymaker Christopher Waller called for more decisive action if price pressures continue to rise. Markets now estimate the probability of a 25-basis-point rate hike in December at 97.3%, with the chance of a 50-basis-point move at 2.7%.

In the UK, the situation is less straightforward. The Bank of England expects inflation to accelerate further by mid-2027 due to cumulative cost pressures, but some components of the October CPI proved fairly stable. Against this backdrop, markets have scaled back expectations of a BoE rate hike in December, further limiting support for the pound.

Yields on UK government bonds also fell following the inflation report, with the yield on 10-year gilts dropping to 5.29%. Although headline CPI reached 3.6% year-on-year, markets have become more cautious about further Bank of England tightening, adding to pressure on GBP/USD.

October UK retail sales will be the next key release, with zero month-on-month growth and 1.7% year-on-year growth expected. Stronger-than-expected data could temporarily support the pound, but the fundamental balance remains in the dollar’s favour due to much stronger expectations of Fed tightening.

Technical Analysis

The H4 GBP/USD chart remains in a downtrend. After a reversal in early November, the pair has formed a succession of lower highs and lows while remaining within the descending channel. The MACD signal line is below zero and pointing downwards, indicating continued downward momentum. The nearest target on H4 is 1.3024.

On the H1 GBP/USD chart, the pair rebounded from 1.3078 to approach 1.3125, where it had previously consolidated. For Friday, 20 November 2026, the baseline scenario assumes a test of 1.3125 from below. If resistance holds, a return to 1.3078 is likely. A break below this low would open the way towards 1.3024. Both Stochastic oscillator lines are above 80. A move out of the overbought zone would strengthen the signal for a resumption of the decline, with the 20 mark becoming the next reference point for the oscillator.

After reaching 1.3024, a rebound towards 1.3080 is possible. If the recovery is limited to this area, the next local downside target is 1.2980. This level corresponds to the continuation of the wave on H4 and may be reached beyond Friday’s session. The longer-range target of the downward wave, based on the chart markings, lies at 1.2584 and remains relevant while the trend holds. A close above 1.3125 on the hourly chart would postpone the intraday decline scenario and increase the likelihood of a deeper correction. data.title: Cheaper Gasoline Is Coming
data.description:
James Thorne of Wellington Altus tweeted an important graph and commentary worth reviewing. The US 3-2-1 crack spread, which approximates what a refiner earns by turning three barrels of crude into two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of distillates, has fallen 36% in six weeks, from $65.56 on October 9 to $41.90 on November 17. As he puts it, “the glut has moved downstream.”

The evidence supports his view. Fat profit margins enticed refiners to run at maximum capacity and boost their profits as much as possible. As one would think, with falling crack spreads, gasoline and diesel prices are falling faster than crude as supply rises rapidly. AAA shows the national gasoline price average near $3.75, down roughly 13% in a month, and the gasoline ETF UGA has dropped about 21% month to date. Gasoline futures have fallen about 45% over the last two months from $3.63 on September 24 to its current level of $2.50. Because retail pump prices lag wholesale/futures by weeks, the AAA pump price should fall further.

Over the last four decades, the 3-2-1 spread averages roughly $12 a barrel with a median near $8. On an EIA spot basis, it averaged $68 in September, the richest month since 2006, and even after the sharp drop to the low $40s, it remains well above average. In other words, spreads have plenty of room to decline as refiners still have the financial incentive to produce as much gasoline and diesel as possible.

Gasoline remains more than a dollar above year-ago levels, so annual price comparisons will likely remain inflationary until spring. However, the Fed Funds futures markets are pricing roughly 75 basis points of further tightening. Hiking into falling energy prices looks to us like the Fed is fighting yesterday’s war.

Market Trading Update

Yesterday, we compared Nvidia’s earnings risk to the “safety” premium investors pay for Walmart. Today, I want to return to the Santa Claus rally we discussed in Tuesday’s commentary, but from a different angle. The question isn’t whether it shows up. It’s WHEN.

Goldman’s flow desk made a sharp point this week. Two-month seasonal averages are too blunt for this tape. Their S&P 500 path, going back to 1928, shows a Thanksgiving ramp, a stall in early December, and a second-leg higher. Read off their chart, roughly 80% of the average gain arrives after December 14. We ran the same test on S&P 500 total returns since 2003, and the shape holds.

The sequence makes sense once you look at who is trading. Retail buying and corporate buybacks typically carry stocks into early December. Then the plumbing gets in the way. Many mutual funds set capital gains distribution record dates around the second week of December, and some taxable investors sell ahead of them to dodge the bill. Tax-loss selling peaks. Goldman expects the buyback window to close around December 13, the Fed meets December 8 and 9, and December 18 brings quarterly options expiration. Once that pile-up clears, managers dress up their books for year-end reporting, and the Santa Claus rally gets its second wind.

Here’s where it gets interesting. Since 2010, the December 5 to 14 window has lost 0.27% on average and finished higher in only 7 of 16 years. In most years, it’s a pause. In 2011, 2014, 2015, and 2018, it was a 3%-3.6% hit.

Goldman’s base rates for years like this one, when the VIX starts mid-November at 18 or higher, deserve respect. The median drawdown inside the window was 3%, and the year-end gain averaged just 1.34%. With the S&P 500 closing Wednesday near 7,318, about 6% below its October 6 record, we’re already living part of that script.

We should not dismiss that hedge funds and CTAs are very underweight technology stocks, which does provide a potential tailwind. However, there is always the risk that they choose to remain sidelined through year-end.

Here is how to play the next few weeks.

  • First, don’t chase the Thanksgiving pop. If the ramp shows up, use strength into early December to trim winners back to target weight and rebuild cash.

  • Secondly, put that cash to work into mid-December weakness, ahead of the stretch that historically does the heavy lifting.

That’s the playbook in our Equity Conservative Growth and Equity Aggressive Growth models. The calendar rewards patience, not urgency. Such is the nature of seasonal trading.

Santa usually shows up, but if you lose too much before then, the gift of Christmas doesn’t really matter.

Fed Worries About AI Financing Web

The October FOMC minutes, released yesterday, contain a passage worth focusing on. Per the minutes, most participants “observed that AI-related debt had grown rapidly,” and much of that growth “had taken place through complex and opaque financing structures.”

A few participants noted that AI exposures were “becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms.” They also flagged off-balance-sheet leasing commitments and circular financing among AI firms as potential loss amplifiers.

We wrote about this last week in Nvidia Circular Financing: Who Is At Risk?, where we traced the guarantees, residual value support, and off-balance-sheet lease backstops that Nvidia was providing to support the AI buildout and, in turn, chip purchases. Our conclusion was that the companies most at risk were those like CoreWeave, with high interest rates and seemingly losing access to the capital markets. The Fed agrees.

Here is why this mention in the minutes is important. The Fed does not casually put a sector’s financing structure into its minutes. Describing AI debt as opaque and concentrated moves it from market chatter to a documented financial stability concern, and that may be the first step toward supervisory attention.

The tension between Fed policy and the AI debt is worth appreciating. In the minutes, almost all participants judged that “further action to raise the target range” would “likely be appropriate,” and two members suggested, “an increase of more than 25 basis points could warrant consideration at the next meeting.” The Fed is now identifying a leveraged, opaque, and concentrated credit structure while preparing to raise its cost of funding. We will watch credit spreads, not equity prices, for any potential fallout. The graphic below is courtesy of The Wall Street Journal.

data.title: The Index Looks Fine. The Heat Map Does Not.
data.description:
WallStreetBets does not usually hand you a clean research note. Last night it handed everyone a giant red rectangle.

A Discussion post titled Last 4-month heat map blew up with roughly 4,000 upvotes and hundreds of comments. The picture is the familiar market map: boxes sized by company size, colored by how far prices have moved, and almost every box is blood red. Nvidia (NVDA) sits near 40% below its recent high, while memory names, chip-equipment stocks, and storage names look even worse. Google (GOOGL), Oracle (ORCL), and Caterpillar (CAT) got painted with the same brush.

The original poster put the quiet part in plain English. This has been a crash under the hood, even if the S&P 500 has not tagged a clean 10% drop yet. That line is the whole argument, and my take lines up with it. The headline index can still look like a messy correction while the engine room of this bull market is already in full drawdown. If your portfolio lives in the red boxes, the map is telling you the truth faster than the S&P number on cable.

What the map is actually showing

People argue about start dates on these charts, and they should. A fixed calendar return from July is not the same thing as a fall from each stock's own high over the last few months. When you line the big tiles up against real prices, the honest read is closer to peak-to-now pain inside a roughly four-month window of highs.

Nvidia topped near $239 in early October and recently traded near $146, about a 40% hole from that high. The semiconductor ETF that tracks the group is still roughly a third below its June peak. Intel (INTC) and ARM are about 60% off their early-summer highs, and Sandisk is on the order of two-thirds lower from its June spike. Micron (MU) and the big equipment names that feed the fabs fill in more of the damage.

Now put the polite index next to that mess. The S&P 500, through SPY, is only about 8% under its early-October high near $779. The Nasdaq-100 path is uglier, down about 15% from the same peak week, and the Dow has slipped back under 50,000. None of those index moves match the temperature of a map where the largest technology tiles look like a stop sign. Indexes are averages with weights, so a handful of survivors can keep the headline from looking like a crash while the prior leadership gets cut in half. That gap is the story.

The survivors are doing real work

Look past the loudest red boxes and you can see why the S&P still has people arguing. Apple (AAPL) has barely given back its recent high and is still solidly up on the year. Microsoft (MSFT) has been one of the adult names in the room on a multi-month calendar view even after a pullback from its own peak, and Amazon (AMZN) has been choppy rather than ruined. Those weights matter, because when the biggest household names hold up better than the speculative AI stack, the index can grind lower without ever looking like 2022 on a chart you glance at once a day.

Breadth can rot while the brand-name average keeps its dignity, which is how investors get talked into thinking they own "the market" when they really own last year's winners at this year's prices. Wall Street will call it healthy rotation. Sometimes rotation is real, and sometimes it is a polite word for the old leadership breaking while a few mega-caps still pay the rent for the index.

Why the under-the-hood crash matters

I am not calling for a cartoon collapse from here, and I am not telling you to light your account on fire. I am saying the heat map is a better dashboard than a single percentage on the S&P.

If the bull market of the last few years was sold as an artificial-intelligence buildout story, then Nvidia, memory, equipment, and the software hanging off that spend are not side shows. They are the plot. A world where those names are down 30% to 60% from their highs while commentators shrug at an 8% index drawdown is a world where risk already showed up, and it showed up first in the places that ran the hardest.

The useful part of the Reddit thread is the admission that index calm and portfolio pain can live in the same month. For anyone holding stocks through this, the practical questions are boring on purpose. How much of what you own is the red cluster on that map? How much leverage, direct or through products that sell when volatility rises, sits on top of those names? Do you still have cash if the under-the-hood crash runs longer than the cable segment about it? Forced sellers do not wait for a perfect bear-market label. They sell when the collateral math says sell.

Watch the falsifiers, not the hot takes. If credit stays orderly while chips thrash, you are often watching a leadership break and a positioning unwind. If credit cracks and the index ballast names finally join the red sea, the under-the-hood story becomes everybody's problem. If Apple-and-Microsoft-class ballast keeps holding the average together while the AI stack stabilizes on real earnings rather than hope, the map can heal from the inside without a full capitulation speech.

Bottom Line

The WallStreetBets heat map is loud because it is honest. The S&P can sit about 8% under its peak and still hide a real crash in the AI and semiconductor engine that powered the rally. Trust the red boxes you actually own more than the polite index percentage on TV, and know your leverage before the next leg decides it for you.

data.title: Palo Alto Networks Stock Soars On Strong FCF Guidance - Any More Upside Left In PANW?
data.description:
Palo Alto Networks (PANW), a cybersecurity software subscription company, reported strong free cash flow (FCF) margins and guided to 38% this fiscal year. PANW stock rose 8% on this guidance on Thursday after rising ahead of the results. Could it be worth more?

PANW is at $364.77, up more than 7.0% midday on Thursday, Nov. 19, after rising 9.9% on Wednesday from a recent low of $309.29 on Nov. 17 ahead of the Nov. 18 fiscal Q1 2027 earnings release (ending Oct. 31) after the market closed.

PANW stock - last 3 months - Barchart - Nov. 19, 2026

Moreover, analysts seem to be very positive on the stock. For example, Yahoo! Finance reports that the average price target (PT) of 54 analysts is $405.78, and Barchart's mean survey PT is $398.62. These PTs are only about 8% higher than Thursday's price (11/19).

So, is there much upside left in PANW?

FCF performance and high FCF Margin Guidance

Palo Alto Networks' fiscal Q1 revenue was up 39.25% YoY, and over the past year it rose 30.29%, according to Stock Analysis data.

Moreover, its adjusted free cash flow (FCF rose 13.1% to $1.937 billion YoY. However, its adj. FCF margin fell from 69.2% in Q1 last year to 59.6% in fiscal Q1 2027.

Nevertheless, on a trailing 12-month (TTM) basis (which is important since many of its clients renew subscriptions annually), the adj. FCF rose almost $1 billion from last year.

This can be seen on page 31 of its presentation deck. It shows that TTM adj. FCF rose from $3.75 billion last year to $4.638 billion in Q1 (+23.5%). It was even 5% higher than the Q4 TTM figure.

Palo Alto Networks - Adj. FCF trailing 12 months (TTM) - Q1 deck page 31 - Nov. 18, 2026

Note, however, that the TTM adj. FCF margin dipped slightly to 37.3% from 39.3% of revenue last year and even 38.4% in fiscal Q4.

However, management provided a 38.0% adj. FCF guidance for the year ending July 31, 2027. Let's see how that might work out. 

Forecasting FCF and Price Targets

Management expects its revenue to be between $14.52 billion and $14.57 billion. That's even higher than prior analysts' average forecasts of $14.4 billion.

For the next year, these analysts forecast $16.47 billion in revenue. So, over the next 12 months (NTM), revenue could be about $15 billion:

  $14.55b x 0.75 + $16.47b x 0.25 = $10.91b +$4.12b = $15.02 billion NTM revenue

So, applying a 38% margin, adj. FCF could hit $5.708 billion

That's over $1 billion higher than the $4.638 billion TTM figure shown above. In other words, its forecasted NTM adj. FCF could rise over 23%.

That certainly shows why the stock is up so much. But, how much is left?

For example, Palo Alto Networks' adj. FCF yield has averaged about 2.0% over the last year (i.e., a 50x multiple). So, applying this metric to its NTM adj. FCF forecast:

  $5.708 / 0.02 = $285.4 billion fair value

That's only about 2.5% above its present market cap of $278.32 billion today. And that implies a PT of $372.30. That's lower than other analysts' targets, as I showed above.

Even with a slightly better 1.85% FCF yield (i.e., a 54x multiple), the stock is worth just $308.54 billion, or +10.9% higher. That gives it a NTM price target of $402.81.

Summary and Conclusion

Palo Alto Networks produced strong adj. FCF with lower quarterly margins, including slightly lower TTM adj. FCF as a percent of revenue (37.3%). As a result, with management's guidance of 38% margin this year and applying this to a next 12-month (NTM) revenue forecast, its adj. FCF could hit $5.7 billion.

With a generous 54x multiple, that only implies a 10.9% higher price target for Palo Alto Networks. Nevertheless, the stock could exceed this at any time. 

But value investors have to take this into account when deciding whether its recent rise leaves any upside.

Anthropic ANT priced its Nasdaq IPO at $83, opened at $111.50 on Nov. 19 and gave back most of that opening gain by Friday morning.

If you missed the offering, three familiar stocks already have a financial stake in what happens next.

Nvidia (NVDA) can benefit when cloud providers buy chips to run Claude.

Amazon (AMZN) and Alphabet (GOOGL) own Anthropic shares and sell it computing capacity.

For investors deciding among the three, the distinction is where the payoff comes from: hardware sales, cloud revenue or appreciation in Anthropic’s stock.

Nvidia sells the hardware behind Claude

Nvidia Corp (NVDA) was among seven companies that bought Anthropic shares in a $26 billion private placement that closed Friday at the IPO price.

Its hardware exposure reaches further.

Anthropic’s prospectus identifies Nvidia-powered capacity under agreements with SpaceXAI and Nscale, alongside its work with Microsoft (MSFT) Azure.

That gives Nvidia several routes to benefit if Claude needs more computing power, even when Anthropic rents that capacity from someone else.

The distinction matters: a cloud provider’s contract value includes services beyond the GPUs, and Anthropic also uses rival chips from Amazon and Google.

For Nvidia shareholders, the number to watch is how much of Claude’s next wave of demand turns into orders for Nvidia systems.

Amazon has an equity stake in Anthropic

Amazon Inc (AMZN) combines an ownership stake with one of Anthropic’s clearest spending commitments.

The IPO prospectus says Anthropic agreed to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon from May 2026 through April 2036, with a provision to pay the shortfall if actual spending falls below the minimum, subject to certain exceptions and adjustments.

The partnership also puts Amazon’s in-house Trainium chips to work training and deploying Claude, while AWS customers can access the models through Bedrock.

For those invested in AMZN shares, the spending floor makes the commercial tie easier to quantify than the equity upside. What ultimately matters to earnings is how much AWS keeps after paying to build and operate the capacity.

Alphabet offers exposure through a stake, chips, and cloud

Alphabet Inc (GOOGL) bought $10 billion of Anthropic’s nonvoting shares in Friday’s private placement, funding part of a prior investment commitment.

Alphabet also benefits through Google Cloud, which offers Claude to enterprise customers through Vertex AI, and through Google’s custom tensor processing units, or TPUs.

Anthropic’s expanded agreement with Google and Broadcom (AVGO) calls for several gigawatts of next-generation TPU capacity expected to start coming online in 2027.

That gives Google shareholders an immediate exposure through the stake and an operating payoff that builds as capacity comes online.

It also gives Alphabet Inc. a large outside customer for its chips – a business opportunity that can grow even when Anthropic’s share price has a rough day.

data.title: The Big Picture: When The Math Finally Breaks
data.description:
If you’ve been listening to our broadcast over the years, you know I often remind our listeners of an old rule of thumb: Wall Street is paid to sell you the next hot story, but math is the only thing that never lies.

Right now, the financial press is obsessed with the AI bust and the Fed’s next move. Will they raise rates a quarter or half a point in December? Will that be followed by further hikes in January and March? Currently, the futures market is forecasting a 97% quarter-point increase in December, a 70% quarter-point hike in January, and a 46% quarter-point rise in March. But the market is probably going to force a pivot.

If you step back from the current headlines and look at the big picture, the more important story isn’t really about the Fed or even AI. It’s that the U.S. government is heading straight into a wall of debt refinancing in 2027—and the numbers simply no longer add up.

The 2027 Debt “Maturity Wall”

Imagine a family that went on a massive spending spree back in 2020. Fortunately for them, the bank offered a special introductory promotion: zero-percent interest for five years.

For five years, that family felt rich. They bought whatever they wanted, and their monthly credit card statement looked tiny because their interest rate was practically zero.

Then the promotion ends. The teaser rate expires, and the bank informs them that their borrowing rate is now adjusting to 22%.

Suddenly, even if they don’t buy another single thing, their monthly interest payment alone eats up half their paycheck.

Sound familiar? What happened to homeowners in the 2000s is precisely what is now happening to the U.S. government.

During the 2020–2021 pandemic crisis, the Treasury borrowed trillions of dollars at rock-bottom rates between 0.5% and 1.8%.

Now those 5-year and 7-year IOUs are coming due.

Through the rest of this year, over $1.1 trillion in older, low-rate debt has to be paid off and replaced with brand-new debt.

In 2027, the dam really breaks: approximately $3.4 trillion in medium- and long-term notes come due. When you include short-term Treasury bills, the government will have to roll over close to $9 trillion in a single year.

Here’s the catch: the Treasury can’t borrow at 1% anymore. Today, it must pay close to 5% or more.

For twenty-five years, whenever Uncle Sam rolled over old debt, it did so at lower rates. Monthly payments went down. Today, that dynamic has flipped. Refinancing that mountain of debt at today’s rates adds tens of billions of dollars every single year to the deficit purely through higher interest costs.

The Snowball Effect: Looking at the Real Numbers

In fiscal year 2026, total government spending topped $7.4 trillion. But look at where that money went: net interest on the national debt jumped over 11% to roughly $1.14 trillion. Net interest is now bigger than our entire national defense budget.

Entitlements are on autopilot: Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid ate up another huge chunk of the budget.

According to the nonpartisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO), our total national debt is blowing past $40 trillion this year. By 2030, debt held by the public will cross 108% of GDP.

To put that into historical perspective: the highest debt level America ever reached was 106% of GDP in 1946, right after mobilizing the entire nation to fight and win World War II. We are on track to permanently shatter that wartime record in peacetime—with no world war, no national draft, and no emergency mobilization.

By 2036, the CBO projects interest payments alone will cross $2.1 trillion a year. At that point, Social Security, healthcare programs, and interest on the debt will consume virtually every single penny of federal taxes collected. Every other department—from the military to the FBI to national parks—will have to be put on the national credit card.

Why Washington Won’t Fix It

You might ask: won’t politicians in Washington just cut spending or raise taxes to fix this?

I’ve watched Washington for over forty years in my career. Neither party has the stomach for real fiscal discipline.

When you look at the major spending proposals on Capitol Hill—whether it’s expanded family tax credits, universal childcare subsidies, healthcare expansions, or housing grants—we are looking at another $3.6 to $4.4 trillion in gross spending programs over the next decade.

Even if you pass every proposed tax increase on corporations and high earners, it barely makes a dent against the compounding wave of interest and baby-boomer retirements. The structural annual deficit will still run at nearly 6% of GDP as far as the eye can see.

The Economy Today: A Tale of Two Consumers

Now let’s look at the economy. Are we about to fall into a deep recession tomorrow?

The economic indicators we watch—like the Conference Board’s Leading Economic Index (LEI)—are actually telling us that growth is holding up around 2%. The job market isn’t falling off a cliff.

Instead, we have a two-track, K-shaped economy.

The Strained Main Street Consumer: If you make an average paycheck, life feels expensive. Prices are up anywhere from 30% to 50% (or higher) since 2020. Credit card debt is at record highs, car loan delinquencies are climbing, and mortgage rates above 7% have frozen the housing market.

The Booming Industrial and AI Pipeline: On the other side of the tracks, money is pouring into artificial intelligence data centers, rebuilding our aging electrical power grid, domestic energy production, and military manufacturing.

This capital-spending boom is keeping the economy afloat. But it has a weak spot: it requires enormous amounts of cheap electricity, expensive equipment, and heavy borrowing. If interest rates stay high, those big corporate projects will eventually hit a wall, too.

The Big Question: When Does the Fed Blink?

Wall Street consensus says the Fed will start cutting rates by mid-2027 because inflation will magically drift down to its 2% target.

I don't buy that inflation story, and neither do many of the sharp macro thinkers we follow.

They point out that the Fed is trapped in a condition economists call Fiscal Dominance. In plain English: the government’s debt has grown so massive that the central bank can no longer control the steering wheel.

Think about the trap Fed Chairman Warsh is in.

If he keeps rates high to fight inflation, he bankrupts the Treasury by forcing them to refinance trillions of dollars at 5%, while crushing regional banks and corporate borrowers.

If he slashes rates, he pours gasoline on inflation, crude oil spikes higher, and consumer prices take off again.

Furthermore, Luke Gromen points out an incredible paradox: when debt is this high, high interest rates fuel inflation. Why? Because the federal government is paying out over $1.1 trillion in cash interest directly into the financial system, putting fresh purchasing power right back into circulation!

So, what happens next? Grant Williams describes it as a forced capitulation. The Fed won’t cut rates because they “won” the inflation fight. No, they will cut rates because the Treasury market will force them to.

We’ve seen this movie before. In the late 1940s, after World War II, the U.S. government had a 106% debt-to-GDP problem. Did they raise interest rates to 10% to fight inflation? Absolutely not.

The Fed stepped in and capped interest rates at 2.5%, while inflation ran at 6%, 8%, or even 10%.

That is called Financial Repression. The government intentionally holds interest rates below the rate of inflation, slowly eroding the purchasing power of cash and bonds to shrink the debt in real terms. It’s a hidden tax on every saver in America.

Your Survival Guide: How to Invest for What Lies Ahead

So, how do you protect yourself when the game is rigged to erode paper money?

For decades, the standard advice was the “60/40 portfolio”—put 60% of your money in stocks and 40% in government bonds, then sit back and retire. In an era of fiscal dominance, that strategy is broken. Long-term government bonds yielding less than the real cost of living are guaranteed to lose purchasing power.

The Financial Playbook My Firm Is Following for Clients

  1. Own Businesses with Real Cash Flow, Not Promises
    In a high-rate world, companies that don’t make money today are toxic. Move money away from debt-heavy, speculative tech stocks trading at nosebleed valuations. Focus on Defensive Value: Healthcare, Consumer Staples, Utilities. These are companies that sell everyday necessities, generate hard cash today, and pay reliable dividends.

  2. Overweight Energy and Master Resources
    Energy is the lifeblood of everything we do. Between geopolitical strife in the Middle East and the massive electric power demanded by new AI data centers, global energy supplies are tight. Owning oil, gas, and power infrastructure gives your portfolio an ironclad inflation hedge.

  3. Demand Clean Balance Sheets
    Avoid companies drowning in junk debt. When that 2027 refinancing wall hits corporate America, weaker businesses will see their profit margins crushed by higher interest costs. Stick with companies with little to no debt and ample cash reserves.

  4. Don’t Panic into 100% Cash
    A lot of frightened investors throw their hands in the air and move everything into cash. That’s a mistake. While cash pays a decent nominal return today, financial repression guarantees that inflation will outrun cash over time. Plus, with corporate share buybacks running hot and short-sellers heavily short, markets can stage violent rallies when you least expect it.

  5. Hold Real, Tangible Assets: Gold
    If history teaches us one undeniable lesson, it is this: whenever governments find themselves with too much debt, they always choose to debase the currency. They have done it from ancient Rome to 18th-century France to post-WWII America.

Physical gold is nobody’s liability. It cannot be printed by a central bank, and it cannot be defaulted on by a politician. In an age of financial repression, gold remains the ultimate monetary anchor.

The Bottom Line

You don’t need to fear the future, but you do need to understand the rules of the game we are playing.

The 2026–2027 debt wall is a mathematical certainty. Washington cannot borrow trillions of dollars forever without consequences, and the Federal Reserve will eventually be forced to choose between defending its currency or bailing out the Treasury.

Keep your head clear, tune out the daily market cheerleaders, avoid debt-choked companies, and anchor your wealth in tangible, cash-flowing assets.

Until next time, stay disciplined, stay safe, and always keep your eye on the Big Picture.

data.title: Bitcoin Falls With Stocks Again: A Link That Only Began In 2020 Is Getting Tighter
data.description:
Bitcoin dropped to $61,291 on November 20, extending a slide that started when US stocks peaked on October 6. Since that day, the largest crypto has lost 28%, while the Nasdaq Composite is down 13.5% and the S&P 500 8.2% through Thursday’s close.

On Thursday alone, the day Anthropic listed on Nasdaq, the S&P 500 fell 2% for its sixth straight loss, and BTC slipped under $62,000.

The two markets are falling in step, and that wasn’t always the case. We measured how closely BTC and the Nasdaq have moved day to day since 2015. For its first years, Bitcoin went its own way. Since 2020, it has traded more and more like a tech stock, and over the past 40 trading days the link has been stronger than in any full calendar year.

So which stocks are hurting most, and why does crypto now fall with them?

AI and Crypto Stocks Lead the Sell-Off

We checked how 45 large AI, chip and crypto-related stocks have done since the October 6 peak. The worst performers fall into a few groups, and most of them sit right where AI and crypto overlap:

  • Miners turned AI landlords: bitcoin miners that now rent their power and buildings to AI companies fell the most. Bitdeer is down 69%, IREN 65%, Cipher Mining 58% and CleanSpark 53%.

  • AI cloud firms: Nebius lost 61% and CoreWeave 51%. Both rent out Nvidia chips to AI customers.

  • Crypto treasury companies: firms that hold crypto on their books dropped about twice as much as BTC itself. Strategy fell 48%, SharpLink 48% and BitMine 43%.

  • Crypto platforms: Galaxy lost 44%, Coinbase 41%, Robinhood 39% and stablecoin issuer Circle 38%.

  • Chips: Arm is down 41%, Nvidia 39% and Micron 34%.

The biggest names held up far better. Microsoft is down 6%, Tesla 2%, Amazon is flat and Apple is up 5%.

Nvidia is at the center of the AI slide. CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week amid a personal scandal, and the chipmaker has lost $735 billion in market value since it broke, the Associated Press reported. Worries that AI stocks had run too high added to the pressure. So did new US limits on remote access to advanced chips and talk of curbs on new data centers after this month’s midterm elections. “The market was already worried about this risk before what happened at Nvidia,” Zhiwei Zhang, chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, said.

Rates aren’t helping either. The 10-year Treasury yield sits above 5%, and inflation is running at 3.1%.

Bitcoin and the Nasdaq Barely Moved Together Before 2020

To answer whether crypto and stocks always moved together, we compared BTC’s daily price changes with those of the Nasdaq Composite, year by year since 2015. The measure, called correlation, runs from 1 (always moving together) to 0 (no link) and -1 (always moving in opposite directions).

  • 2015 to 2019: the correlation stayed between -0.11 and 0.08. The coin rose and crashed on its own news, with almost no tie to stocks.

  • 2020 onward: it jumped to 0.45 in the Covid year and has stayed positive since, peaking at 0.60 in 2022, when rising interest rates sank both markets.

  • Not a straight line: the link loosened to 0.19 in 2023, then climbed back to 0.47 in 2025.

  • Right now: over the last 40 trading days, it reached 0.65, above any full calendar year. The record for a 40-day stretch is still 0.81, set in May 2022.

So the answer is no. Crypto and stocks didn’t always move together. It’s a habit that started in 2020 and has grown stronger this year.

Big Investors Now Hold BTC Next to Tech Stocks

Several changes since 2020 explain why Bitcoin now trades like a risky tech stock:

  • The same buyers: hedge funds, wealth managers and pension funds now hold BTC, often through exchange-traded funds (ETFs) launched in January 2024. When they cut risk, they tend to sell both crypto and tech at once.

  • The same fuel: cheap money pushed both markets higher in 2020 and 2021. Higher rates pulled both down in 2022, and the prospect of more rate hikes is weighing on both now.

  • The same companies: many listed firms now straddle both worlds. Miners host AI data centers, and treasury companies like Strategy trade as stocks while holding crypto.

That last group shows the link most clearly. When AI shares fell, the miners that rent space to AI firms fell harder than either the coin or Nvidia.

Bitcoin Price Analysis: $62,300 Is The First Test For Bulls

On the daily chart, BTC trades at $61,859. That is below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $74,655, and its 200-day EMA at $75,470.

  • Resistance: $62,300, the floor BTC held in June, July, August and twice this month, now acting as a ceiling. Above that, $65,500.

  • Support: $58,500, where BTC turned in June and again on July 1.

BTCUSDT 1D chart. Source: TradingView

As long as Bitcoin keeps moving with the Nasdaq, the next clue for BTC may come from tech stocks, starting with Nvidia. A calmer week for AI shares would give $58,500 a better chance to hold. Another leg down in tech would likely drag crypto with it.

data.title: Gold And Silver Reverse At My $3,522 And $41.22 Targets
data.description:
In Gold Trading Alerts, my targets for gold and silver futures were $3,522 and $41.22. Overnight, gold fell to $3,514.90 and silver to $41.02.

At the moment of writing these words, December gold futures trade near $3,570, and December silver futures trade near $42.15. Both reversed from their overnight lows, which were their lowest levels since September 2, 2025, and the gold-to-silver ratio is at about 84.8, its highest level since October 2025.

These targets weren't new, and neither was the reasoning behind them.

Gold and Silver Reach My Targets

On November 2, when December gold futures traded near $3,950 and silver futures near $51, I outlined these downside targets for my Gold Trading Alerts subscribers in the summary part of the Alert: $3,522 for gold futures and $41.22 for silver futures. Overnight, gold futures moved down to $3,514.90, $7.10 below their target, and silver futures moved down to $41.02, 20 cents below theirs. Then both reversed. Since November 2, gold has declined by about 10 percent and silver by about 18 percent.

The $41.22 target for silver futures was a trader-friendly version of the Fibonacci-based target of about $40.90, and silver reversed only 12 cents above it.

In my view, a correction might be upon us in both metals.

My free analyses pointed to the same area. On October 30, when silver traded near $49 and the gold-to-silver ratio was about 79, I wrote about the ratio: "I expect it to rise toward the 80-84 range of the previous bottoms. With gold at about $3,500, this would put silver at about $42-$44." On November 4, when silver traded near $52, I repeated it in my silver forecast: "silver is likely to move toward $42-$44." The ratio is now slightly above the upper border of that range, and since November 4, silver has declined by about 19 percent.

The two targets for silver describe the same move: the $41.22 level corresponded to gold futures at their $3,522 target, so with gold at its target, silver was likely to be slightly below its November target area. That's where it reversed.

A question from one of my subscribers shows what's happening in the physical silver market at the same time.

What Silver's Backwardation Means

One of my Gold Trading Alerts subscribers asked in the comments whether it means much that silver is in backwardation right now. It's a good question, and I'm happy to answer it here as well.

Backwardation means that silver for immediate delivery costs more than silver for later delivery. Normally, the futures trade above the spot price, because they include the cost of financing and storing the metal. This morning, spot silver traded slightly above the December futures, while the January and March contracts traded above December. So the front of the curve is inverted, and it shows that some buyers want physical silver now and are willing to pay up for it.

In my view, it doesn't change the outlook. The price of money is what drives silver right now, and a tight physical market didn't prevent a sharp decline last year either: in October 2025, London was so short of metal that buyers struggled to find it, and silver still fell about 15 percent from its October 17, 2025 high to its October 28 low.

The price of money shows up in the dollar first.

The USD Index Is Close to Its Next Target

On September 1, when gold traded near $4,426, I wrote: "Yesterday was the third day in a row when the USD Index closed above its declining resistance line. This means that the breakout was confirmed." The USD Index closed at 99.68 that day. Since then, it has risen by about 4 percent, while silver has fallen by more than 35 percent.

On Thursday, the cash USD Index closed at 103.89, its highest close since April 1, 2025.

In my view, the next target for the USD Index is at about 104.2-104.3. That's where the 61.8 percent Fibonacci retracement of the 2025-2026 decline and the previous high are. The USD Index is relatively close to this area, so it could jump to it sharply and then reverse within a day or so. Given the current technical position of the precious metals and stocks, I don't think that the USD Index will be able to prevent their rebound.

The Fed's officials keep the pressure on. On Thursday evening, Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson said that the Fed will need to raise interest rates again because inflation is too high, and the fed funds futures price the December 9 hike as practically certain.

That's silver's monetary side. Its industrial side got some relief overnight.

Copper Reverses at Its 50% Retracement

Industry is the biggest source of silver demand, and much of that silver goes into electrical uses, the same kind of uses that drive copper demand. That's why copper's moves matter for silver investors.

Overnight, December copper futures moved down to $5.4405, and copper reversed after correcting to the 50 percent Fibonacci retracement level. A temporary bottom might be in.

The copper producers fell hard before this reversal. FCX's stock price fell 4.53 percent on Thursday, to $49.12, its lowest close since December 18, 2025.

A temporary bottom isn't the end of the decline, though, and two markets point to more weakness later on.

Why the Upswing Is Likely to Be a Bull Trap

The first is the stock market. On Thursday, the S&P 500 fell for the sixth day in a row, as Anthropic's shares failed to hold their early gains. Please note that during massive multi-market declines, stocks tend to decline for longer than the precious metals. In the 2008 financial crisis, gold bottomed on October 24, 2008, while the S&P 500 bottomed only in March 2009. In 2020, gold bottomed on March 16, and the S&P 500 on March 23. That's why, even if silver and gold formed their short-term bottoms today, stocks could still drop a bit more.

The second is crude oil. At the end of October, WTI crude oil traded above $100, and overnight, the January WTI futures moved down to $80.78, 7 cents above their September 4 low. The decline in the price of crude oil doesn't have to help stocks and other commodities. After crude oil moved decisively above $100 in 2008 and in 2022, stocks, the miners and FCX plunged later on, even if it didn't happen immediately, and when it happened, they declined along with crude oil.

This chart also shows how far stocks and commodities are likely to decline in general, and stocks have barely started their decline. This matters for silver, because as an industrial metal, it gets sold when stocks and commodities slide. That's why I think that the corrective upswing will be a so-called bull trap. Many will think that the decline is over and that this was a short-term correction within a bull market, but I don't think so. In my view, the main top of the long-term rally in stocks and commodities is in.

This view is connected to another question from the comments.

Another one of my Gold Trading Alerts subscribers asked whether there are any circumstances in which the low that we might see later this month becomes the final bottom, and whether anything in the next few months could change my view about where gold's decline is most likely to end. It's a good question, and I'm happy to answer it here as well.

In short, such circumstances are possible, but I don't see them right now. Today's low might be the short-term bottom, but in 2013, the April low wasn't the final one either: gold corrected and then fell further, to its June 28 low. In my view, the final bottom will form when gold reacts less and less to the dollar's strength and when the miners and silver lead gold higher. I still think that the final bottom is likely to form much lower.

Where This Leaves Us

Gold and silver futures moved below my $3,522 and $41.22 targets, and both reversed, along with copper. In my view, a corrective upswing in the precious metals sector is likely to start now, even if the USD Index moves up to about 104.2-104.3 first. Stocks could fall a bit longer, though, and crude oil's long-term chart points to much lower prices for stocks and commodities, so I think that the upswing will be a bull trap. In today's Gold Trading Alert, I described how far I think silver, gold and the miners could correct, and the trades that I'm making for this upswing.

In 2013, silver's April low didn't hold either: by late June, silver was about 14 percent lower.

data.title: Preliminary Regional Fed Manufacturing Reports Suggest Inflation Is Spreading Downstream
data.description:
In discussing the ISM manufacturing index several weeks ago, I concluded that it “reminded me of the regional Fed reports for the last month, which suggested that while the expansion is intact, the second derivative may be declerating, i.e., the rate of growth has been peaking; and further that its inflationary component is accelerating, which is not good for downstream consumer prices.”

Here’s what the new orders component of that index looked like:

Well, now we have three regional Fed bank reports for November: New York, Philadelphia, and Kansas City, which give us our first look at how manufacturing is doing this month. The first two do get picked up by FRED, so let’s see what their averages can tell us.

First of all, the headline numbers (bue) declined -6.2 to 7.0, which suggests at least that the growth rate is stabilizing and possibly decelerating somewhat.  But, unlike the ISM report at the beginning of this month, the average of the new orders component (red) was the lowest since last year, as it decelerated sharply, by -12.4, to 1.3:

Meanwhile, the respective numbers from the Kansas City Fed constrasted significantly, as the headline regional index rose 7 to 18, and the new orders component rose 13 to 16.

Put all three together and the picture is of a stabilizing topline, and at very least the proverbial bloom might be coming off the rose somewhat as to new orders.

There might be an even more significant amplification present is in the prices component, and specifically prices received from downstream customers (red in the graph below). Prices paid declined -1.3 to 52.0, suggesting the torrid spread of price increases in that component has persisted. But even more signficantly, prices received rose 1.2 to 37.1. The last two months have been the highest readings in that entire series since the start of the Millennium outside of the post-pandemic period:

The regional Kansas City index suggested the same, with prices paid declining -17 to 53, and prices received rising 4 to 30.

In short, producers appear more determined, and able, to pass on higher prices to downstream customers, suggesting that consumer inflation, at least in the goods sector, is not going to slow in the next several months, and may even increase further. And keep in mind that real aggregate nonsupervisory payrolls may go negative YoY as early as next month if there is such a pass-through of inflation and a tepid employment report. In that regard, the best news in the surveys was that employment average rose 5.4 to 1.8:

All well and good for the present, but if corporate profits come under pressure, and real wages come under pressure as well, needless to say that would not be good.
