data.title: Inflation Takes On A Life Of Its Own Independent Of Oil Prices
data.description:
Driving by the local gas station, motorists are taking a sigh of relief as pump prices have declined rapidly in recent weeks—-- a reflection in the hope for a US-Iranian peace agreement will put  an end  to the disruptions in the oil market. Bond investors, reacting to the prospects of future inflation, however continue to drive up yields, and central bankers talk up the need to curb inflation with higher rates for longer. The once tight correlation between oil prices, inflation and government bonds is coming apart. 

Historically, oil price shocks, such as those in the 1970s and 1980s, had an immediate effect of driving up prices across the board. At the same time, the drop in oil prices resulted in a rapid decline in the rate of inflation—-- a sharp doubled-edge sword. Today, inflation expectations  seem to be well-anchored, such that despite a drop in the oil prices, consumer inflation seems very slow to react, putting central bankers on alert towards raising rates.

Earlier in the year, the  tight correlation between oil and government borrowing costs has defined global bond markets,as the long end of the credit markets everywhere hit highs not experienced in over a decade. So, central bankers blamed the geopolitical situation for the need  to raise rates, emanating from the Iranian conflict. But that conflict is in abeyance and oil is now flowing through the Straits of Hormuz close to pre-war levels 

Starting in 2022,  the correlation between oil prices and interest rates averaged around 25%, yet interest rates climbed steadily from 1.8% to 4%, as central banks moved off the ultra-low rates that characterized the 2020s. With the advent of the Iranian conflict,  oil prices spiked from $65/bbl to $120/bb, accompanied by a surge in  the 10-year yield  from 4.2% to 5.1%. Current estimates put the oil-interest rate  correlation at 20%-25%.

But despite steep falls in global crude benchmarks in recent weeks — in part on hopes for US-Iran peace talks — yields and expectations for rate rises have remained elevated, keeping up the pressure on governments’ and households’ finances. Central banks are focusing on a raft of conditions to guide their deliberations, and the oil prices seem to play a lesser role in their minds. Inflation is no longer confined to specific commodities, but is more generally pervasive, pushing the central bankers to tighten further.

data.title: Bitcoin’s Latest Crash Has A Silver Lining
data.description:
Recently, I explained how the midterm elections could impact the future of AI.

But artificial intelligence wasn’t the only technology affected by this month’s political shakeup.

The cryptocurrency industry spent more than $170 million trying to influence the midterms, backing candidates who promised to support digital assets and establish clearer rules for the industry.

And while many of those candidates won their races, Democrats ultimately won control of both houses of Congress.

That prompted reader MK to write in and ask:

Now that the Democrats have taken over the government, do you think that the future of crypto is going to go to the bottom or at least [go] in that direction as we have seen in the past few days after the election?

The answer isn’t as simple as you might think.

The midterms certainly created more uncertainty for the crypto industry. And with prices continuing to fall, I understand why investors are worried.

But I also believe this selloff could create some excellent buying opportunities.

Crypto’s Next Chapter

For the past several years, cryptocurrency companies have been fighting for something that most other industries take for granted.

Clear rules about how they can operate.

You see, cryptocurrencies don’t fit neatly into America’s existing financial regulations. Some digital assets function like investments. Others are used to make payments, power blockchain networks or provide access to financial services.

And for years, regulators have disagreed over which government agencies should oversee them.

But last year, Congress finally started making progress.

In July 2025, lawmakers passed the GENIUS Act, creating the first federal regulatory framework for stablecoins.

As I’ve noted before, stablecoins are cryptocurrencies designed to maintain a steady value, usually by being tied to the U.S. dollar. They allow people and businesses to transfer money using blockchain networks, often much faster than traditional banking systems.

Congress also took up another major piece of legislation called the CLARITY Act.

This bill would establish clearer rules for cryptocurrency exchanges and determine which digital assets fall under the Securities and Exchange Commission and which fall under the Commodity Futures Trading Commission.

The House passed the bill in July 2025 with bipartisan support. But it stalled in the Senate.

And now, with Democrats preparing to take control of Congress in January, its future is even more uncertain.

Some lawmakers want stronger consumer protections and tougher restrictions on cryptocurrency businesses.

But I don’t think the Democrats are going to spend the next two years trying to shut down an industry that has become an important part of the financial system. They also have to consider the economic consequences of making America a less attractive place for cryptocurrency companies to operate.

So I believe there’s still room for compromise, even if new legislation takes longer than the industry had hoped.

Of course, investors haven’t been waiting around to find out what Congress will do. They’ve been selling.

And it’s only gotten worse since the election.

Bitcoin (BTC) briefly fell toward $62,000 last weekend, and Ethereum (ETH) has also taken a beating, falling below $2,000 and trading near $1,800.

And, frankly, I think we could see even more selling before the market finds its footing.

Part of the reason is that cryptocurrencies have become closely connected to technology stocks. When investors sell tech stocks, they often sell their cryptocurrencies too. And that can send prices falling even faster.

Investors are also worried about rising interest rates, and money has been flowing out of bitcoin investment funds. Both have added pressure to an already nervous market.

So I wouldn’t be surprised to see bitcoin fall further and trade within a relatively narrow range for a while.

But my long-term outlook hasn’t changed.

I still see bitcoin as an alternative to the dollar, especially as government debt continues to grow. And I’m particularly optimistic about Ethereum, which I believe could outperform bitcoin as the market recovers.

Meanwhile, companies are finding new ways to put cryptocurrencies to work.

For example, BitGo recently announced that its institutional clients can earn bitcoin rewards through Stacks (STX), a project that allows developers to build financial applications using bitcoin.

And they can do it without moving their bitcoin out of BitGo’s custody.

That’s a big deal because it makes it easier for large financial institutions to earn rewards on their bitcoin holdings.

And that’s exactly the kind of progress I look for when evaluating cryptocurrency investments.

I want to see projects that are actively developing their technology, signing new deals and finding ways to attract more users.

Because even when prices are falling, those are the developments that can create opportunities for investors.

Here’s My Take

I’ve been following cryptocurrency long enough to know that market selloffs can create enormous opportunities for patient investors.

Of course, not every cryptocurrency will recover. But I’ve already identified several projects that I believe have enormous long-term potential.

In fact, I’ve recommended Ethereum and Stacks to subscribers of my Next Wave Crypto Fortunes service because I believe both could play an important role in the future of finance.

[Editor’s Note: Want to know which cryptocurrencies Ian King believes could deliver big gains as the market recovers? Call 877-422-1888 to learn more about his Next Wave Crypto Fortunes service and how you can get access to his latest recommendations.]

That said, I expect more volatility for a while.

The Nasdaq could continue pulling crypto prices lower. And Washington may take longer than investors hoped to establish clearer regulations.

But crypto will keep moving forward, regardless of what happens in Congress.

And I’m convinced investors who focus on that progress could be richly rewarded in the years ahead.

data.title: Private Credit Redemptions: Why Investors Still Can’t Get Out
data.description:
Private credit redemptions are falling, but most funds still return only 5% of shares per quarter.

Key Takeaways

  • Redemption requests at the largest non-traded private credit funds are easing, but most still pay out only 5% of shares per quarter.

  • At Blue Owl’s flagship OCIC, most third-quarter requests came from investors resubmitting orders that went unfilled earlier in the year.

  • The demand was built when cash paid nothing. In nine of the twelve years from 2010 through 2021, the 3-month T-bill averaged below 0.5%.

  • Listed BDCs, which get a daily market price, trade at a median of about 88 cents per dollar of reported net asset value.

  • The better question for an investor is whether you’ll need the money before the line clears.

The headlines say private credit redemptions are easing. They are. In the third quarter, investors asked to pull $4.2 billion from Blue Owl’s two largest non-traded credit funds, down from $4.7 billion in the second quarter and a record $5.4 billion in the first.1 However, both funds still bought back just 5% of their shares, the same as every other quarter this year. Such is the part of the story most coverage skips. Fewer investors are heading for the exit, but the ones already in line are still standing there.

That matters to anyone who owns one of these funds or got pitched one over the last few years. The pitch was income with “semi-liquid” access. Income has shown up. For a lot of people, access hasn’t.

“Semi-Liquid” Means Liquid Until Everyone Wants Out

Non-traded business development companies (BDCs) and interval funds don’t trade on an exchange. You get out when the fund offers to buy back your shares, usually once a quarter. That offer is typically capped at 5% of shares outstanding. When requests exceed the cap, the fund prorates. In other words, everyone who asks gets the same fraction of their request filled, and the remaining shares stay put.

Ares Strategic Income Fund shows how that works in practice. In its third-quarter tender, investors submitted roughly 50.4 million shares, and the fund bought about 19.3 million of them, or 38.2% of each request.2 Holders with fewer than 100 shares got paid first. Everyone else waited.

Seven of the ten non-traded BDCs tracked by Crowdfunded Wealth prorated their latest completed offering, filling between 12.8% and 49.9% of investors’ requests.3 The three that paid in full simply had fewer people asking. Notice that none of this is a default. The gate is NOT a malfunction. It’s written into the prospectus. And it’s working exactly as designed, which is precisely the issue if you need the cash. A gate that protects the fund from a fire sale, by forcing it to sell loans into a weak market at whatever price a buyer will offer just to meet withdrawals that came in faster than the loans can mature, is the same gate that keeps you from your money. It cuts both ways.

Why Are Private Credit Redemptions Still Being Prorated?

A question that keeps landing in my inbox goes something like this: “If requests are falling, isn’t the problem fixed?” Not quite. Fewer requests mean a shorter line. They don’t mean a wider door.

Look at Blue Owl Credit Income Corp. (OCIC), a $35 billion fund. Requests ran at 21.9% of shares in the first quarter, 18.8% in the second, and 16.8% in the third.1,4 That’s improvement. Yet Reuters reported that most third-quarter requests came from investors resubmitting tenders that hadn’t been filled earlier in the year.1 Such is how a queue works. The people asking to leave in September are largely the same people who asked in June.

For a better understanding of what this means, let’s run the arithmetic. At a 5% quarterly cap, a 16.8% line takes roughly three and a half quarters to clear. That assumes nobody new joins it. OTIC, the smaller tech-heavy sibling, saw requests hold near 39% of shares. At the same pace, that’s nearly two years. Blackstone’s BCRED, the largest of the group, received tenders for about 181 million shares in its third-quarter offer, roughly 10% of shares outstanding. It bought back about 90 million of them, or 49.9% of each request, for $2.13 billion.5

There are exceptions. KKR’s FS Income Trust Select saw requests of 5.06% and paid every one, stretching slightly past its cap.6 That’s a fund with under $1 billion in net assets and a small overage. The arithmetic changes when the line is three times the door.

How TINA Built The Line At The Exit

To understand why the line formed, you have to go back to where the money came from. For most of the decade after the financial crisis, the Fed held short rates near zero. Savers who needed income had two choices: accept nothing on cash or seek “yield” elsewhere. Wall Street called it “TINA,” for “there is no alternative.” It pushed a generation of conservative money further out on the risk curve than it had ever been.

As is always the case, when there is a LOT of investor demand, Wall Street will find a way to capitalize on it. Private credit was the perfect product for that environment. It paid high single-digit to low double-digit distributions. The reported value barely moved because the loans weren’t marked to market every day. Investors saw a “smooth” line and concluded it was safe. That’s the confusion. Low reported volatility and low risk are different things, and illiquidity is the cost that never shows up in the monthly statement. Howard Marks put the general version of this better than anyone:

“The riskiest thing in the world is the widespread belief that there’s no risk.” – Howard Marks, Oaktree Capital Management

Now flip the setup. As of November 12, the 3-month bill yields 4.32%.7 My colleague Michael Lebowitz recently laid out how investors have moved from TINA to TIGA: “there is a good alternative”. When cash pays four percent with daily liquidity, the extra few points from a gated loan fund look a lot less compelling. Some of today’s private credit redemptions reflect credit worry. Much of it, I suspect, is investors doing that math for the first time.

The Strongest Case For Staying In

The other side of this debate has real merit. The underlying loans are mostly performing. At Ares Capital, the largest listed BDC, loans on non-accrual were 2.4% of the portfolio at cost as of September 30, up from 1.8% at year-end but hardly a collapse.8 The Fed called the risks tied to private credit redemptions “manageable” back in May.9 Evercore’s Glenn Schorr said the industry “it appears that the industry has successfully isolated the direct lending wound.”1

The gate also protects the investors who stay. Back in March, I made this case in Subprime Crisis 2.0: Will Private Credit Be The Trigger? Gating and a mostly institutional investor base, I argued, make this look more like a painful credit cycle than a 2008-style collapse. I still think that’s right. Distributions keep arriving while you wait, and nobody is forced to dump loans at distressed prices.

“A gate is a promise kept to the fund. It’s a promise deferred to you.”

So the case for staying is real. The cost is just as real: you’ve handed the timing of your exit to a tender schedule. For an investor with a long horizon and no near-term need for the money, that may be a fair trade. For one who planned on this as a source of spending money, the trade looks very different.

What Listed BDCs Say About Private Credit Redemptions

There’s a useful cross-check here. Listed BDCs hold the same kind of loans to the same kind of middle-market companies. The difference is that they trade on an exchange every day. Their price shows what investors will actually pay for a dollar of those loans today. A non-traded fund’s reported NAV can’t tell you that.

The detail that jumps out is Blue Owl’s own listed BDC, OBDC. It reported a net asset value of $14.32 a share at the end of September and closed November 13 at $10.97, or about 77 cents on the dollar.8,10 Its non-traded siblings transact with redeeming investors at reported NAV, when they transact at all. That doesn’t prove the non-traded marks are wrong. Listed prices carry their own fear premium, and a discount can say as much about sentiment as about the loans. But when the market price and the reported price differ by 10% to 25%, the investor who can only exit at the reported price, 5% at a time, is relying on marks the market won’t confirm.

Buyers are putting their own marks on these loans as well. In November, BC Partners’ listed BCP Investment Corp. agreed to buy Investcorp Credit Management BDC at 90% of its adjusted net asset value. It’s part of a wave of consolidation as smaller lenders look for scale. Ares Capital agreed to acquire MidCap Financial Investment Corp. in late October. When a professional buyer pays 90 cents per dollar of reported loans, that’s information, too.

My colleague Michael Lebowitz walked through why not all BDC yield is created equal, and the same discipline applies here. A discount is information. Deciding whether it’s an opportunity takes more work.

Is Private Credit Safe For Your Portfolio?

The word “safe” is the wrong focus. The much better test is whether the money you invest can sit idle for as long as it takes the line to clear. Start with the timeline. If you may need these funds in the next two years, the queue matters more than the yield. If the money truly is long-term, the gate is an inconvenience rather than a crisis.

More importantly, you should also focus on just how much of your liquid net worth sits behind a gate. A small sleeve of private credit in a large portfolio is one thing. A retirement income plan built around one is something else. Will a tender schedule ever be convenient? No. However, will knowing your exposure keep a gate from becoming a forced decision somewhere else in the portfolio? Absolutely.

Finally, ask what your plan assumes about a bad year. Retirees selling assets during a drawdown already face the problem I described in Sequence of Return Risk: The Math That Breaks Retirements. If the “liquid” sleeve you planned to draw from is gated, you sell whatever else is liquid. Often, that happens at the worst moment. Such is the hidden cost of illiquidity: it rarely hurts the asset that’s locked. It hurts the assets that aren’t.

None of this argues for rushing to tender. It also says nothing about whether any particular fund is a good or bad holding for you. It argues for knowing exactly what you own: the tender calendar, the cap, how proration works, and how long your share of the line might take to clear. Right now, the consensus says the private credit scare is over. It may be. The line is still there either way.

Bottom Line

Private credit redemptions are easing, but the 5% door hasn't widened, so any money behind a gate should be money you won't need until the line clears.

The yield was real. So was the lockup, and plenty of investors are only now reading that part of the brochure.

Questions This Article Answers

Why can't I withdraw my money from a private credit fund?

Most non-traded BDCs and interval funds buy back shares once a quarter, and cap repurchases at about 5% of shares outstanding. When redemption requests exceed that cap, the fund prorates, filling only part of each request. In their latest completed offers, seven of the ten non-traded BDCs tracked by Crowdfunded Wealth filled between 12.8% and 49.9% of requests.

What does proration mean in a private credit tender offer?

Proration means every investor who asked to redeem gets the same percentage of their request filled. In Ares Strategic Income Fund’s third-quarter 2026 tender, about 50.4 million shares were submitted and about 19.3 million were bought, so investors received 38.2% of their request after holders of fewer than 100 shares were paid first. The rest of the shares stay in the fund until a later tender.

Is private credit safe right now?

The underlying loans are mostly performing, and redemption requests have eased since the first quarter of 2026. The bigger risk for individual investors is liquidity. If you may need the money before your place in the redemption line clears, a gated fund can force you to sell other assets at a bad time.

How long does it take to get out of a non-traded BDC?

It depends on how long the line is relative to the 5% quarterly cap. A fund with requests equal to 16.8% of shares, as Blue Owl’s OCIC saw in the third quarter of 2026, would need roughly three and a half quarters to clear the line if no new requests arrived. A fund with requests for nearly 39% of its shares would need almost two years.

data.title: Disaster Survival Stocks: Companies That Could Benefit When Americans Prepare For The Worst
data.description:
The recent wave of technology outages, airline groundings, and disruptions to critical services has given Americans something new to think about: How prepared are we if the systems we depend on every day suddenly stop working?

On November 13, 2026, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) experienced a telecommunications network failure that resulted in a nationwide ground stop. The disruption lasted approximately four hours and 45 minutes, with more than 12,000 flight cancellations reported that day. The problem affected 17 of the FAA’s 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers. Although the FAA said that all aircraft landed safely, the incident demonstrated how a technical failure in one critical system can disrupt transportation across the country. 

There have also been other unsettling developments. United Airlines experienced a separate technology outage that disrupted flights at several major airports, including San Francisco International Airport. Meanwhile, the National Security Agency (NSA) experienced an outage of its internal classified information network on November 17. The NSA attributed the disruption to scheduled maintenance, and officials said there was no evidence of a cyberattack. Nevertheless, the incident raised questions about the reliability of even highly sophisticated government computer systems. 

These events have fueled concerns about how vulnerable modern society has become to technology failures, cyberattacks, power outages, natural disasters, and interruptions in essential services. People increasingly recognize that electricity, communications, transportation, banking, and food distribution systems are interconnected. A problem in one area can quickly affect many others.

For investors, this raises an interesting question: Are there publicly traded companies that could benefit financially if more Americans begin preparing for emergencies?

There is an investment theme that could be called disaster survival stocks. These are companies that manufacture or sell products people may want to have available when normal services are interrupted. They include generators, emergency supplies, canned food, bottled water, home improvement products, ammunition, and other necessities.

The recent events have also brought renewed attention to a group of people known as preppers.

The Prepper Movement Goes Mainstream

Preppers are people who take steps to prepare for emergencies, ranging from relatively ordinary situations such as hurricanes, earthquakes, and extended power outages to more extreme possibilities such as widespread infrastructure failures, economic disruptions, and societal breakdowns.

Traditional preppers often maintain supplies of food and water, backup electricity, first-aid equipment, emergency communications devices, and other necessities. Some have installed solar panels, battery storage systems, and generators. Others maintain gardens, preserve their own food, store fuel, and develop plans for living without conventional utilities.

What is particularly interesting is that emergency preparedness is no longer limited to people who consider themselves survivalists.

A November 19, 2026, Washington Post report described Americans buying emergency supplies following the recent outages. Purchases included bottled water, canned food, battery-powered radios, portable generators, solar power stations, and propane supplies. One consumer reportedly spent approximately $3,500 expanding his emergency inventory. The article also reported unusually strong interest in generators at Costco, with 21 of the 26 most expensive generators listed on its website sold out as of the preceding Sunday. 

An additional report from Axios described a substantial increase in emergency-preparedness shopping, with one survival-gear retailer reporting a 450% increase in sales between October 27 and November 16 compared with preceding weeks. 

Whether these developments represent a temporary reaction to the headlines or the beginning of a longer-term trend remains to be seen. However, they could create opportunities for companies that supply the products associated with emergency preparedness.

Here are six publicly traded companies that investors and traders may want to investigate.

1. Olin Corporation (NYSE: OLN)

A Chemicals and Ammunition Play

Emergency supplies exposure

NYSE: OLN

Olin is an interesting, somewhat unconventional disaster-preparedness investment because it operates two businesses that could be relevant during periods of heightened emergency preparedness. Its Winchester division manufactures ammunition, including products for recreational shooting, hunting, law enforcement, and military applications. Its other operations produce chemicals, including chlorine, caustic soda, and epoxy products.

Ammunition is an established component of the prepper market, particularly among individuals interested in hunting, personal protection, and self-sufficiency. Increased consumer interest in emergency preparedness could potentially support ammunition demand, although Winchester’s business is much broader than the prepper market.

Olin reported third-quarter 2026 sales of approximately $1.75 billion and net income of $14.4 million, compared with $42.8 million in the prior-year quarter. Adjusted EBITDA was $191.4 million, down from $222.4 million. The company is also pursuing a merger with Huntsman, which it expects to close in the first quarter of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals. 

Investment consideration: Winchester provides an interesting angle on the preparedness theme, but investors should remember that Olin is primarily a cyclical chemical company. Its earnings are sensitive to industrial demand, energy costs, chemical prices, and operating conditions. Its substantial debt and proposed merger also deserve attention.

2. The Home Depot (NYSE: HD)

The Emergency Repair and Equipment Play

NYSE: HD

Home Depot is one of the more obvious companies that could benefit when homeowners decide they need to become more self-sufficient. The company sells generators, power tools, flashlights, batteries, building materials, plumbing supplies, electrical equipment, and other products that become particularly important when homes experience damage or utility interruptions.

After a hurricane, wildfire, earthquake, or extended power outage, homeowners frequently need equipment and materials to restore their properties. Portable generators, extension cords, chainsaws, tarps, water pumps, and electrical supplies can all experience increased demand.

Home Depot also benefits from longer-term trends that have little to do with disasters, including aging housing stock, remodeling, maintenance, and professional contractor spending.

The company reported fiscal third-quarter 2026 sales of $43.4 billion, up 4.9% from the prior-year quarter. Comparable-store sales increased 2.2%, while earnings were $3.72 per diluted share. Management projected approximately 4.5% full-year sales growth for fiscal 2026. 

Investment consideration: Home Depot offers exposure to disaster-related repairs and preparedness without relying exclusively on emergency purchases. However, higher interest rates, weak housing turnover, and reduced consumer spending on remodeling could affect growth.

3. Generac Holdings (NYSE: GNRC)

The Backup Electricity Play

One of the most direct beneficiaries

NYSE: GNRC

Generac may be one of the most direct ways to invest in the disaster-preparedness trend. The company manufactures standby generators, portable generators, battery storage systems, and other energy technology products.

For homeowners, a standby generator can automatically provide electricity when the utility grid goes down. This can be particularly important for people who depend on electricity for medical equipment, refrigeration, heating, air conditioning, security systems, and communications.

The company also sells commercial and industrial backup power systems. Hospitals, data centers, telecommunications facilities, businesses, and other critical operations require dependable backup electricity.

An especially interesting development is the growing demand for backup power from data centers. Generac announced a long-term supply agreement with Amazon that includes an expected $2.4 billion in initial generator deliveries during 2027 and 2028.

Generac’s third-quarter 2026 results were impressive. Net sales increased 16% to a record $1.29 billion, while net income rose to $109 million from $66 million in the prior-year quarter. Residential sales increased approximately 9%, supported by stronger demand for home standby and portable generators. The company maintained its full-year sales growth guidance in the mid-to-high teens percentage range. Its data-center product backlog reached approximately $4.5 billion. 

Investment consideration: Generac is particularly attractive as a way to participate in the longer-term need for backup electricity, including data-center demand. However, the stock can be sensitive to weather patterns, residential construction, interest rates, and the timing of generator purchases. Competition and execution risks associated with its expanding industrial business should also be considered.

4. The Campbell’s Company (Nasdaq: CPB)

The Shelf-Stable Food Play

Nasdaq: CPB

Food is one of the most basic components of emergency preparedness. When people worry about disruptions to grocery stores, transportation, or electricity, they often begin stocking their pantries with products that have long shelf lives.

Campbell’s is well positioned in this category through its soup, canned food, sauces, snacks, and other packaged food products. Its well-known brands include Campbell’s, Prego, Pace, Swanson, and Goldfish.

Canned soup and other shelf-stable foods are particularly useful during emergencies because they can be stored for extended periods and many varieties can be consumed with little preparation.

Unlike companies that sell generators or emergency equipment, Campbell’s has a business that is not dependent on consumers making large discretionary purchases. Food is something people need regardless of economic conditions.

However, investors should be aware that Campbell’s has recently encountered financial difficulties. For fiscal 2026, annual sales declined 5% to $9.7 billion, while adjusted earnings per share declined 27% to $2.17. The company announced a dividend reset as part of a strategy to accelerate debt reduction. It is also targeting $500 million in cost savings by fiscal 2030. 

Investment consideration: Campbell’s offers defensive consumer staples exposure, but investors should not assume that increased emergency food purchases will automatically translate into substantial earnings growth. Competition, consumer preferences, food input costs, and the company’s debt reduction efforts are important considerations.

5. Walmart (Nasdaq: WMT)

The Essential Goods Distribution Play

Nasdaq: WMT

Walmart could be one of the biggest beneficiaries of increased consumer interest in emergency preparedness simply because of its enormous retail distribution network.

The company sells virtually everything consumers might need during an emergency, including bottled water, canned food, batteries, flashlights, first-aid supplies, over-the-counter medications, blankets, coolers, portable power equipment, and household necessities.

Its combination of physical stores, distribution centers, and e-commerce operations gives it an advantage in making essential products available to consumers. Walmart’s grocery business is particularly important because food represents a large portion of household emergency supplies.

There is also an important distinction between Walmart and some of the other companies discussed here. Walmart does not need a major disaster to generate sales. It sells everyday necessities that consumers purchase regularly, regardless of whether they are preparing for an emergency.

Walmart reported third-quarter fiscal 2027 revenue of $188.8 billion on November 19, 2026, an increase of 5.2%. E-commerce sales increased 17% globally, and the company raised its full-year outlook. Operating income increased 16%. 

Investment consideration: Walmart offers a relatively diversified way to participate in the emergency-preparedness theme. Its scale, pricing power, and everyday grocery business provide some defensive characteristics. However, its valuation, labor costs, competitive pressures, and retail profit margins should be examined before purchasing shares.

6. Costco Wholesale (Nasdaq: COST)

The Bulk Purchasing and Stockpiling Play

Recent demand evidence

Nasdaq: COST

Costco might be one of the most interesting companies in this group because its warehouse business is naturally suited to consumers who want to purchase large quantities of essential goods.

Its merchandise includes bulk bottled water, canned food, paper products, batteries, first-aid supplies, household necessities, and emergency equipment. Costco also sells generators and other power-related products.

The membership warehouse model encourages consumers to buy larger quantities than they might purchase at a conventional grocery store. This is particularly attractive to households that want to maintain an emergency supply of food and other essentials.

There is already evidence that recent events have generated increased interest in Costco’s emergency-preparedness merchandise.

According to a November 2026 report citing Mizuho Securities, 21 of the 26 most expensive generators listed on Costco’s website were sold out as of November 15. Analysts also attributed some of the company’s stronger October comparable-store sales to emergency-preparedness purchases. 

Costco reported fiscal 2026 annual sales of approximately $297.2 billion, up 10.1% from the previous year. Fourth-quarter net income increased to approximately $3.0 billion from $2.61 billion. Its October 2026 sales increased 12.6% to $24.5 billion. 

Investment consideration: Costco has an attractive business model, recurring membership income, and a loyal customer base. It could benefit from increased stockpiling, but emergency purchases are only a small part of its overall business. Its valuation is also an important consideration. Investors should avoid assuming that a temporary surge in preparedness shopping justifies paying an excessive earnings multiple.

Other stocks worth investigating

The six companies above are not the only publicly traded businesses that could benefit from increased emergency preparedness.

These companies provide additional exposure to different aspects of emergency preparedness, from portable power and food production to water infrastructure and home repairs.

What Are the Biggest Investment Risks?

Although disaster preparedness is an interesting investment theme, investors should distinguish between a temporary increase in consumer purchases and a sustained change in spending behavior.

A major outage or natural disaster can produce a sudden increase in demand for generators, bottled water, canned food, batteries, and other supplies. However, consumers may already have purchased these products, reducing the need for repeat purchases.

For example, a household that buys a generator may not need another one for 10 or 15 years. Similarly, people who stock their pantries with canned goods may not need to replenish their supplies immediately.

There is also the risk that investors will overreact to headlines. A stock can rise substantially on expectations of higher demand even if the actual increase in company earnings is relatively small.

Valuation is especially important. Costco, for example, has a strong business, but its shares have historically commanded a premium valuation. Campbell’s has a more defensive food business, but its recent financial results illustrate that even companies selling essential products can experience declining earnings.

Finally, these companies are exposed to different economic forces. Olin is affected by industrial chemical demand, Generac by generator purchasing cycles and data-center investment, and Home Depot by the housing and remodeling markets.

Conclusion: Building a Disaster-Preparedness Investment Watchlist

The recent technology outages, airline disruptions, and NSA network incident have highlighted an important vulnerability of modern society: We depend on interconnected systems that can sometimes fail unexpectedly.

Whether these incidents prove to be isolated technical problems or part of a broader trend, they have reminded consumers of the importance of having backup plans.

From an investment perspective, I would put Generac near the top of the list because it provides direct exposure to backup electricity, a market that has opportunities beyond residential emergency preparedness, particularly with data centers. Home Depot is another interesting candidate because it sells the equipment and materials needed to prepare for and recover from disasters.

Walmart and Costco provide exposure to consumers stocking up on necessities, while Campbell’s offers exposure to shelf-stable food. Olin is a more specialized investment, with its Winchester ammunition business providing an additional angle on the preparedness market.

I would be particularly interested in monitoring whether the recent increase in emergency-preparedness shopping translates into sustained sales growth over the next several quarters. If consumers begin making preparedness a regular part of household budgeting rather than simply reacting to alarming headlines, some of these companies could benefit from a meaningful long-term business trend.

The key for investors and traders is not to bet on a disaster occurring. It is to identify companies that sell products people increasingly value because they want to be prepared if one does.

data.title: Labor Department Rewrites Independent Contractor Rules. Wall Street’s Independent Advisors Get A Win
data.description:
Washington has changed the rules again for determining who qualifies as an independent contractor. This time, the independent financial advisory industry has reason to celebrate.

On November 19, the U.S. Department of Labor announced a final worker-classification rule, replacing the broader standard adopted in 2024 with a framework resembling the one introduced in 2021.

For independent financial advisors and broker-dealers, the decision addresses a longstanding concern. Could the regulatory supervision required by securities laws eventually become evidence that an advisor should be classified as an employee?

The new rule makes that distinction clearer.

It also raises familiar questions about worker protections, operating costs and how much independence a contractor actually possesses.

Two Factors Take Center Stage

The Labor Department’s new regulation restores an economic reality test with five factors, placing greater emphasis on two.

The first examines the nature and degree of control a company exercises over a worker.

The second evaluates whether the worker has an opportunity to earn profits or suffer losses through personal initiative or investment.

Other considerations include specialized skills, the permanence of the working relationship and whether the work forms part of an integrated production operation.

The distinction matters because the 2024 rule evaluated six factors without assigning predetermined weight to any of them.

The new framework gives greater importance to entrepreneurial independence.

An individual who controls business decisions, invests personal capital and accepts financial risk has a stronger argument for independent contractor status.

Simply signing an independent contractor agreement does not settle the issue.

The Labor Department says actual working arrangements carry more weight than contractual descriptions.

Apparently, Washington has rediscovered the concept that what people do matters more than what their paperwork calls them.

Why Financial Advisors Are Paying Attention

The Financial Services Institute estimates that approximately 175,000 independent financial advisors represent about 60% of producing registered representatives in the United States.

Many operate their own practices while affiliating with broker-dealers for securities transactions, compliance oversight and operational support.

That arrangement creates an unusual relationship.

Advisors can own their businesses, develop client relationships, hire employees and make entrepreneurial decisions.

At the same time, their affiliated broker-dealers must supervise regulated activities.

The potential problem involves distinguishing legally required supervision from the type of business control associated with employment.

The new regulation clarifies that complying with certain legal obligations, including securities regulations, does not itself demonstrate employer-like control.

That is particularly significant for independent broker-dealers.

Without the distinction, firms could face greater uncertainty over whether mandatory compliance procedures undermine advisors’ independent status.

Financial Services Institute Celebrates

The Financial Services Institute welcomed the final rule.

FSI President and CEO Dale Brown described independent financial advisors as entrepreneurs who choose to build businesses and serve clients in their communities.

The organization argues that clearer classification standards help preserve the independent advisory model.

FSI supported the proposed rule earlier this year and previously challenged the 2024 regulation in federal court.

The industry’s position is understandable.

Independent broker-dealers have built substantial businesses around relationships with affiliated advisors who operate independently rather than as traditional employees.

Changing that classification could affect compensation arrangements, administrative responsibilities and operating costs.

The new rule reduces one source of federal regulatory uncertainty.

It does not eliminate every legal question surrounding independent advisory relationships.

The Financial Stakes Are Significant

Worker classification has direct financial consequences.

Employees can qualify for minimum wage, overtime and other employment protections that generally do not apply to properly classified independent contractors.

Companies also face different payroll, administrative and benefit obligations depending on employment status.

Reuters reported that employees can cost businesses substantially more than contractors, citing surveys suggesting differences reaching 30%.

That figure is a broad cross-industry estimate, not a forecast of savings for financial advisory firms.

For broker-dealers, the economic implications depend on individual affiliation agreements, compensation structures and actual working relationships.

A change in classification could require adjustments to staffing, payroll administration and compliance procedures.

But the new rule does not automatically convert employees into contractors or authorize firms to avoid legitimate employment obligations.

Classification still depends on the facts.

Worker Advocates See a Different Problem

Business groups have welcomed the change, but worker advocates remain concerned.

Critics argue that giving greater weight to entrepreneurial factors could make it easier for businesses to classify economically dependent workers as independent contractors.

That concern extends well beyond financial services.

Trucking, healthcare, retail and app-based delivery businesses also rely heavily on contractor arrangements.

A worker classified incorrectly can lose access to important wage-and-hour protections.

The Labor Department maintains that its revised framework provides clearer standards while preserving protections for individuals who qualify as employees.

The disagreement reflects a fundamental policy question.

How should regulators distinguish genuine business ownership from employment arrangements structured to avoid labor obligations?

There is no universal answer based solely on job titles or contractual language.

What the Rule Does Not Change

The new framework applies to worker classification under the Fair Labor Standards Act and two related federal laws, the Family and Medical Leave Act and the Migrant and Seasonal Agricultural Worker Protection Act.

It does not rewrite Internal Revenue Service classification standards.

It also does not override state or local employment laws.

That distinction is important for financial firms operating across multiple jurisdictions.

An advisor’s classification under federal wage-and-hour regulations does not necessarily determine the outcome under every other applicable law.

Broker-dealers must continue evaluating their relationships against relevant state requirements, federal tax rules and securities regulations.

The final rule becomes effective 60 days after publication in the Federal Register.

Until then, firms have an opportunity to review agreements and operating practices.

What Independent Broker-Dealers Should Do Next

The most practical response is a review of existing advisor relationships.

Firms should examine who controls business decisions, who bears operating expenses, how compensation works and whether advisors exercise genuine entrepreneurial independence.

They should also distinguish mandatory securities supervision from discretionary business management.

Written agreements should accurately reflect how relationships operate in practice.

Compliance departments and employment counsel should coordinate rather than treating worker classification as an isolated human resources issue.

The regulation provides a clearer federal framework, but documentation and actual conduct remain essential.

A Regulatory Win, With Limits

The Labor Department’s decision is a meaningful development for the independent financial advisory industry.

It recognizes that required securities supervision does not automatically eliminate entrepreneurial independence.

That clarification supports the business model used by many independent advisors and broker-dealers.

But the broader worker-classification debate is far from settled.

Federal tax requirements, state laws and disputes over individual working arrangements remain.

For now, independent advisors have received something increasingly valuable in financial regulation.

A clearer definition of the rules governing their businesses.

Whether Washington leaves those rules alone long enough for everyone to get comfortable with them is another question entirely.

Naples, Florida, November 20th, 2026, FinanceWire


Artificial intelligence is moving deeper into medicine, and cancer care is emerging as an important area of application. Machine learning models are being used to detect cancer earlier, help doctors select treatments, and monitor patients for signs of recurrence. Increasingly, these capabilities are being developed around a simple blood sample.

The companies building large AI models are pushing further into the field as well. Anthropic (NASDAQ:ANT) recently outlined how its Claude models are being incorporated into real-world drug development programs. In one example, six scientists at Generate Biomedicines used Claude Code to redesign a component of CAR T-cell therapy. The new design, about 70% shorter than the standard version, produced roughly 10 times as many receptors in lab tests and killed tumor cells more efficiently.

Meanwhile, blood-based cancer testing is moving beyond development and into commercialization. Tests are already available for colorectal cancer screening, multi-cancer early detection, and monitoring tumor DNA after a diagnosis. Newer approaches, including infrared spectroscopy, are also being developed to detect multiple cancer types from a single blood draw. Here are five stocks to take a closer look at.

DataMEDS AI, Inc. (NASDAQ:MEDS) is a healthcare technology company integrating pharmacy, laboratory, and telemedicine operations through its EinsteinRx AI platform. Its Helomics subsidiary operates a CLIA-certified precision oncology laboratory in Pittsburgh, built around the ChemoFx assay, which evaluates how a patient's live tumor cells respond to different chemotherapy agents. The company is now looking to expand its cancer diagnostics capabilities through blood-based testing and artificial intelligence.

DataMEDS has agreed to acquire certain assets from Todos Medical, including its Total Biochemical Infrared Analysis (TBIA) cancer testing platform and three tests: TM-B1 and TM-B2 for breast cancer, and TM-C1 for colorectal cancer. The acquisition introduces another approach to cancer detection that could complement Helomics' existing precision oncology capabilities.

TBIA uses Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy to analyze the biochemical characteristics of blood plasma and peripheral blood mononuclear cells. The platform digitizes the resulting data and applies machine learning to identify patterns that may distinguish healthy individuals from patients with cancer. Rather than relying exclusively on individual biomarkers detected through antibodies, the technology analyzes broader biochemical signatures. This approach could eventually support the detection of multiple cancer types and disease states using a single blood draw.

DataMEDS plans to install the spectroscopy platform at Helomics, where it can draw on the laboratory's existing infrastructure and oncologist network. The company intends to correlate TBIA results with biopsy and imaging data, conduct validation work, and pursue a commercial launch as a laboratory-developed test. It also sees potential for subsequent FDA submissions as the platform and its applications advance. The agreement additionally includes Todos Medical's license for the LymPro Alzheimer's diagnostic blood test.

Guardant Health, Inc. (NASDAQ:GH) is developing blood-based diagnostics across the cancer care continuum, including its Shield test for colorectal cancer screening. FDA-approved in 2024, Shield analyzes cell-free DNA for genetic and epigenetic changes associated with cancer. Guardant also offers precision oncology tests that help guide treatment decisions in patients with advanced cancer. Its third-quarter 2026 Shield volume reached approximately 83,000 tests, up 246% year over year, highlighting the growing adoption of blood-based screening.

GRAIL, Inc. (NASDAQ:GRAL) is focused on multi-cancer early detection through its Galleri test, which analyzes cell-free DNA from a single blood sample for cancer-associated methylation patterns. Machine learning helps identify potential cancer signals and predict their likely tissue of origin, guiding follow-up testing. Galleri is designed to detect signals associated with more than 50 cancer types, including cancers without widely recommended routine screening programs. GRAIL reported more than 56,000 tests in the third quarter of 2026, approximately 24% above the prior-year period, while an FDA advisory committee recently voted in favor of the test's safety, effectiveness, and overall benefit-risk profile.

Natera, Inc. (NASDAQ:NTRA) approaches cancer diagnostics through molecular residual disease testing. Its Signatera platform uses tumor-specific genetic information to track circulating tumor DNA in a patient's blood following a cancer diagnosis. This allows physicians to monitor for molecular signs of residual disease or recurrence that may not yet be visible through conventional imaging. Natera is also developing AI models that combine genomic sequencing, digital pathology, and longitudinal patient data to improve recurrence prediction. Oncology testing volume increased 60.9% year over year in the third quarter of 2026.

Freenome, Inc. (NASDAQ:FRNM) is developing blood-based cancer screening through a platform that combines artificial intelligence, machine learning, and multiomics. Its SimpleScreen CRC test received FDA approval in July 2026 for colorectal cancer screening in average-risk adults aged 45 and older, with Abbott holding exclusive U.S. commercialization rights. Abbott launched the test commercially in September, and Freenome launched SimpleScreen Lung in October. The company is also developing a broader multi-cancer detection approach, with an initial readout expected in mid-2027.

As AI becomes more integrated into pharmaceutical research and cancer diagnostics, these companies illustrate how the technology is being applied across different stages of medicine, from developing new treatments to detecting cancer, guiding therapy, and monitoring patients after treatment.

data.title: Equities Decline For Seventh Session In A Row, As Tech Rout Deepens On Total AI Avoidance
data.description:
The S&P 500 is declining for the seventh consecutive session as the tech rout extends amidst a huge amount of derisking occurring here on Wall Street. The Nasdaq 100 is down nearly 4% and has effectively erased its year-to-date gains, as investors rapidly unload AI exposure in consideration of the monumental risks on the horizon. First off, a Jensen-less Nvidia (NVDA) is worrying participants about the lack of an influential hype-man that can support the sector during times of anxiety, like in the current moment. Additionally, investors are concerned that Asian momentum will decelerate in light of the space’s China avoidance, posing headwinds to revenue and earnings prospects. The blue sweep in the midterm election, which handed significant majority controls of both chambers of Congress to the Democrats, is also generating jitters pertaining to heavier regulations and stricter oversight. The four major US stock benchmarks are tanking as a result, but 5 of the 11 principal sectors are advancing while capital allocators lift exposures to the defensive consumer staples, healthcare, utilities and real estate categories, as well as the energy segment, even as oil prices decline on strengthening Middle East crude exports. Cheaper fuel alongside heavy safe-haven demand is plunging yields by more than double-digits at the short-end, contributing to the Treasury curve descending aggressively in bull-steepening motion, as the odds of a one-and-done hike by the Fed to end the current tightening cycle rises meaningfully. That dovish tilt is weighing on the greenback, while deteriorating sentiment crushes cryptocurrencies and commodities but lifts premiums on volatility protection instruments substantially, with the VIX exceeding 32, its highest level since March.

At Risk of a Down Year

Wall Street is at risk of having its first down year since 2022, which also happened to feature a midterm election and Fed rate hikes. But with the dramatic collapse from fresh equity records occurring a little over six weeks ago, a prolonged period of lackluster stock returns could be upon us. It could be the case, that the bull market could have ended in October, as serious doubts about AI’s ability to power corporate earnings and the economy forward are reflected via punishing repricing occurring across shares and fixed-income assets. And with risks piling up, investors are seeking free cash flow yields from these massive capital expenditures more than ever; nonetheless, the nosebleed expectations that drove this theme into the stratosphere amidst elevated potential of a meaningful slowdown have created too wide of a gap for overall firms to satisfy participants at this juncture.

International Roundup

China Holds Key Interest rates

The People’s Bank of China decided this morning to keep its one- and five-year prime rates unchanged at 3% and 3.5%. Those generally accommodative rates have been in place for more than a year with the central bank seeking to juice weak domestic demand. The central bank has maintained the current rate for slightly more than a year.

Retail Sales Strengthen in the UK

Retail sales volumes in the UK strengthened in October and exceeded economist consensus estimates, according to preliminary data from the Office for National Statistics. Consumer shopping grew 0.7% month over month (m/m) and 2.3% year over year (y/y) following September’s 0.6% slip and anemic annual gain of only 0.4%. Economists estimated that October would post no monthly change and a y/y gain of only 1.7%.  Pain at the pump caused purchases of automobile fuel to fall 2.2% by volume last month. The contraction dragged down the broad headline result. Indeed, the core retail sales metric, which excludes auto fuel, was up 0.9% m/m and 2.5% y/y. Both metrics strengthened from September’s 0.9% m/m descent and anemic 0.4% annual gain. At the same time, they easily exceeded the economist consensus expectations for a 0.1% m/m dip and a 0.7% y/y ascent. For the monthly headline print, sales at other non-food stores, textile clothing and footwear, non-store retailing and food stores climbed 3.1%, 1.5%, 0.9% and 0.8%. Department stores and household goods stores experienced declines of 1.2% and 1%.

But In Mexico, Retail Activity Weakens

Mexican consumers trimmed their spending in September by 0.3%, which matched the economist consensus estimate and weakened considerably from the preceding month’s strong 1.2% expansion. Sales were still 2.2% higher than in the year-ago period. Nevertheless, the y/y result decelerated from 3.3% in August and missed the economist consensus prediction of 2.7%.

And Canada Experiences Sales Decline

The value of retail transactions in Canada is expected to have sunk 1.5% m/m in October, according to a preliminary estimate from Statistics Canada. The result is based on responses from 58.1% of companies that were surveyed. Statistics Canada also provided final data for September. In that month, the value of cash register transactions was up 0.8% m/m. Sales were up in five of nine subsectors, led by increases at gasoline stations and fuel vendors.

data.title: Markets Reassess The AI Growth Story For 2027
data.description:
Artificial intelligence has become an increasingly important engine of U.S. economic growth, helping to fuel a surge in spending on data centers, semiconductors, networking equipment, and the energy infrastructure needed to power them. At a time when other sectors have shown signs of slowing, the race to build AI capacity has supported business investment and provided a meaningful lift to economic activity.

That strength, however, may also represent a potential vulnerability. If AI-related investment begins to cool, whether due to overcapacity concerns, weaker returns, financing constraints, or a shift in corporate priorities, one of the economy’s most dynamic sources of growth could fade, exposing a greater dependence on a relatively narrow segment of business spending.

To date, the AI buildout has been a strong net plus. Apollo chief economist Torsten Slok estimates that “AI investment added roughly 1.3 percentage points to real GDP growth over the last three quarters, or about 65% of the roughly 2% cumulative growth, led by software and computers.” That makes AI “the number one source of growth for the US economy, and anyone making statements about the 2027 outlook for equity and credit markets is implicitly making assumptions about the pace and magnitude of the AI data center buildout.”

For the upcoming fourth-quarter GDP report, the AI buildout is still expected to be a positive force for economic growth. How long this tailwind lasts, and to what degree, is quickly becoming a focus of debate as tech stocks and the broad equity market continue to slide. The S&P 500 Index tumbled 2% on Thursday and is now down more than 8% since Oct. 6, when the benchmark closed at a record high.

For now, at least, the outlook for economic activity in the October-through-December period remains relatively upbeat. U.S. growth is projected to rise at an annualized 2.9% rate in Q4, based on the median estimate of a set of nowcasts compiled by The Capital Spectator. That’s a moderately softer pace than the 3.4% increase reported for Q3, but the nowcast for the current quarter still points to a faster pace than the mid-2% trend in the first half of the year.

Today’s median Q4 estimate reflects a slight downshift from our previous 3.1% nowcast on Nov. 9. Momentum in the economy is still strong enough to tilt the odds in favor of a solid gain for the current quarter, but questions about what’s in store for 2027 are increasingly coming into focus.

That uncertainty is becoming more visible in asset prices. Equities have retreated this month, leaving the S&P 500 Index at its lowest level since April. Meanwhile, the bond market is benefiting from renewed demand for safe-haven assets, lifting government bond prices and pushing yields lower. The rebound in fixed-income buying reflects a growing debate over whether economic growth will cool in 2027, a development that could also help ease inflation pressures.

Artificial intelligence has been a powerful tailwind for both the economy and the stock market, driving investment, boosting productivity expectations, and fueling a rally in technology shares. More recently, however, investors have begun questioning whether the enormous sums being spent on AI infrastructure and data centers will generate returns sufficient to justify the costs. The resulting shift in sentiment has triggered a broad selloff in tech stocks and raised concerns that one of the economy’s strongest growth drivers may be losing momentum.

The stock market is not the economy, but markets are forward-looking and tend to price in expectations for future growth. The recent decline in stocks, particularly AI-related shares, alongside falling Treasury yields, suggests investors are becoming less confident that the forces underpinning today’s economic resilience will be as powerful in 2027. Whether that concern is justified remains unclear, but it helps explain why investors are taking a more cautious view of the year ahead.

data.title: PayPal Stock Falls As Leadership Shake-Up Tests Turnaround Strategy
data.description:
PayPal stock PYPL fell 4% on Friday after the payments company announced a series of leadership changes as part of its turnaround efforts under CEO Enrique Lores.

The appointments include a new chief financial officer and executives overseeing consumer financial services, payments and artificial intelligence operations.

The company said the changes follow several months of strategic planning aimed at clarifying priorities across its core businesses, simplifying its operating model and strengthening leadership accountability.

However, the management overhaul comes as investors remain cautious about PayPal's ability to revive growth and regain market share.

PayPal has lost about 7% over the past 12 months.

The stock has also fallen approximately 82% from its all-time closing high of $308.53 reached on July 23, 2021.

PayPal appoints new CFO and business heads

Claire Bramley, currently CFO of cloud-based accounting software provider Xero, will join PayPal as executive vice president and CFO on February 1, 2027.

She will replace Jamie Miller, who has served as chief financial and operating officer.

Bramley will work with Miller during February to support the transition.

Bramley previously held senior finance positions at HP, where her tenure overlapped with Lores.

PayPal also appointed Kartik Mani as president and head of Consumer Financial Services and Venmo.

Mani joins from American Express, where he was president of Global Network and Partner Services. Venmo general manager Alexis Sowa will continue in her role and report to him.

Suzan Kereere, who currently leads PayPal's Global Markets business, will become president and head of Payment Services and Crypto.

She will succeed Jeff Pomeroy, who had been serving as interim head and will continue leading Payment Services and Platforms, reporting to Kereere.

Juan Rio will join the company on November 30 as executive vice president of AI Business Transformation and Operations.

He previously worked at Brightstar.AI as managing director and chief delivery officer. Rio will oversee AI initiatives, cost simplification and enterprise operating effectiveness.

Separately, PayPal announced that Chief Risk Officer Aaron Webster would leave the company.

Ratinder Bedi, senior vice president of Credit and Fraud Risk, will serve as interim head of the risk organisation while PayPal searches for a permanent replacement.

Board appointment and investor concerns

PayPal also appointed Brian J. Lee to its board of directors, effective November 30, 2026.

Lee served as Goldman Sachs' chief risk officer from 2019 to January 2025 and most recently chaired its Risk Council through October 2026.

The leadership changes come as Wall Street analysts remain divided over PayPal's prospects.

Of the 45 analysts covering the stock, 31 have a Hold rating, seven recommend selling, and seven have a Buy rating.

Monness Crespi Hardt analyst Gus Galá recently downgraded PayPal to Sell from Neutral and set a $48 price target.

He cited market-share losses and unfavourable business trends, including a year-over-year decline in third-quarter transaction revenue from PayPal's products and services.

Analysts at Freedom Broker, Cleveland Research and Bank of America have also recently downgraded the stock.

Analysts assess PayPal's growth engines

Not all analysts are negative on the company. Susquehanna analyst James Friedman maintains a Positive rating and a $67 price target.

Friedman believes PayPal's growth prospects should not depend entirely on its traditional branded checkout business.

He identified buy now, pay later services, Venmo, and Braintree's value-added merchant tools as three newer growth engines, each of which has recorded double-digit growth.

He argued that the traditional checkout business may only need to achieve modest growth of 2% to 3% to support overall profit expansion.

Friedman also expects PayPal to treat 2027 as an investment year, directing spending towards these three growth areas while using internal cost savings to keep overall earnings steady.

The turnaround, which Lores has led since joining in March, has focused on cost reductions and greater adoption of artificial intelligence.

PayPal's fourth-quarter results, expected in early February, will provide investors with an opportunity to assess management's progress.

Forward guidance and updates on the turnaround strategy are likely to remain central to the market's assessment of the company's new leadership team.
